stories.headline: Thanksgiving nor’easter leaves hundreds of thousands without power and gives Central Park its wettest Thanksgiving on record
stories.deck: A powerful coastal storm hit the East Coast on Thursday, Nov. 26, flooding shore towns, cancelling hundreds of flights and knocking out power to more than 850,000 customers by late evening, according to NBC News’ count from PowerOutage.us. Central Park logged 1.82 inches of rain, its wettest Thanksgiving on record.
stories.summary: A powerful coastal storm hit the East Coast on Thursday, Nov. 26, flooding shore towns, cancelling hundreds of flights and knocking out power to more than 850,000 customers by late evening, according to NBC News’ count from PowerOutage.us. Central Park logged 1.82 inches of rain, its wettest Thanksgiving on record. The Washington Post called it the worst Thanksgiving Day storm on the East Coast in decades, with 60 to 70 mph gusts from North Carolina to New York, major bridges closed and damage reported in Hampton Roads, coastal New Jersey and the Washington–Baltimore area. As of 11:50 p.m. ET, NBC listed more than 184,000 customers without power in Pennsylvania, 169,000 in New Jersey, 131,000 in Maryland, about 96,700 in Virginia and 76,000 in New York; a separate snowstorm left about 92,000 without power in Missouri. FlightAware counted more than 450 cancellations and 2,400 delays by 10 p.m. ET, with JFK, LaGuardia, BWI, Reagan National and Boston Logan among the hardest hit. In suburban Maryland, WSSC Water asked about 1.9 million customers to use water only for essentials after power problems at two treatment plants. The National Weather Service’s New York office said the previous Central Park Thanksgiving record was 1.72 inches, set on Nov. 23, 2006. The 100th Macy’s parade, postponed because of the storm, is scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 28.
stories.why: Outage counts were still changing overnight, so expect repairs, flight backlogs and flooded low-lying streets to linger into the weekend, including for Black Friday travel and Saturday’s rescheduled parade. A storm this strong on one of the busiest travel days of the year also tests how well utilities and airports cope.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: Follows the Nov 26 edition, which reported the storm’s arrival and the parade postponement. Outage totals change hour by hour and differ by tracker and time: the Post reported more than 700,000 during the storm, NBC more than 850,000 at 11:50 p.m. ET. A Reuters report carried by Investing.com could not be opened this morning (access limit) and is not cited.

stories.headline: Black Friday arrives with forecasts of record online spending, as surveys show shoppers hunting for value
stories.deck: Retail forecasters expect strong online sales over the Black Friday–Cyber Monday stretch, but surveys cited by CNBC show shoppers squeezed by prices and concentrating spending into sales. The National Retail Federation expects about 126 million people to shop on Black Friday itself.
stories.summary: Retail forecasters expect strong online sales over the Black Friday–Cyber Monday stretch, but surveys cited by CNBC show shoppers squeezed by prices and concentrating spending into sales. The National Retail Federation expects about 126 million people to shop on Black Friday itself. The NRF’s survey, released Nov. 19, found 182.7 million people planned to shop between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, down from 186.9 million last year, as more people start holiday shopping earlier. CNBC reported on Friday morning that Adobe counted $82.5 billion in U.S. online spending in the first 22 days of November, up 9.1% from a year earlier, and that Salesforce forecasts $84 billion in U.S. online sales for Nov. 24–30, up 6%. A Deloitte survey cited by CNBC found 87% of shoppers planned to buy during Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales, the highest share since 2016, with Gen Z especially keen on deals. These are forecasts and surveys; actual sales figures come later.
stories.why: Holiday shopping is a big read on how households are coping with prices: spending can still rise while people buy fewer things or wait for discounts. If you are shopping, many “Black Friday” deals began days ago, so comparing prices is still worth it.
stories.label: Reported + Industry figures
stories.note: All figures are company or industry forecasts and surveys, not final sales data.

stories.headline: Thanksgiving NFL: Bears win at Detroit with 3 seconds left, Eagles erase a 21-point deficit in Dallas, Bills beat Chiefs in the rain
stories.deck: The NFL’s Thanksgiving tripleheader on Nov. 26 produced three one-score games: Chicago beat Detroit 39–35, Philadelphia beat Dallas 39–38 and Buffalo beat Kansas City 13–10 in the nor’easter.
stories.summary: The NFL’s Thanksgiving tripleheader on Nov. 26 produced three one-score games: Chicago beat Detroit 39–35, Philadelphia beat Dallas 39–38 and Buffalo beat Kansas City 13–10 in the nor’easter. In Detroit, Caleb Williams hit Rome Odunze for a 6-yard touchdown with three seconds left, which NFL Research called the latest go-ahead touchdown in a Thanksgiving game since at least 1970; the 9–2 Bears now lead their division. In Dallas, the Eagles were down 31–10 in the third quarter before backup quarterback Joe Milton III threw for 331 yards and three touchdowns, with DeVonta Smith catching 11 passes for 200 yards; NFL.com called it the largest comeback in Thanksgiving history. In Orchard Park, Tyler Bass kicked a 57-yard field goal in driving rain and Harrison Butker missed from 46 as the Bills (10–1) won a low-scoring game in which Josh Allen passed for just 81 yards but James Cook ran for 117.
stories.why: Thanksgiving football is one of the most-watched slots of the season, and these results reshape the playoff race: Chicago is now ahead of Detroit, and Buffalo stays on top of the AFC. The Bills game also showed how far the storm reached beyond the coast.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: AP’s recap could not be opened this morning (access limit) and is not cited; results are from NFL.com and the Buffalo Bills’ own site.

stories.headline: Hunger Games prequel on course to lead the Thanksgiving box office as Disney’s Hexed and Focker-in-Law open softer
stories.deck: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping made about $15.1 million on Wednesday, Nov. 25, and is projected to take around $85 million over the five-day holiday, according to The Hollywood Reporter. Disney’s animated Hexed and the Meet the Parents sequel Focker-in-Law opened with smaller numbers.
stories.summary: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping made about $15.1 million on Wednesday, Nov. 25, and is projected to take around $85 million over the five-day holiday, according to The Hollywood Reporter. Disney’s animated Hexed and the Meet the Parents sequel Focker-in-Law opened with smaller numbers. Francis Lawrence’s adaptation of Suzanne Collins’s 2025 prequel, with Joseph Zada as a young Haymitch Abernathy, opened to $119 million in North America last weekend and would reach roughly $233 million domestically by Sunday if the projection holds. Hexed, a $200 million-plus original animated film, took an estimated $7.6 million on its first day including previews, with THR pointing to a five-day start around $35 million, below the studio’s earlier hopes; Focker-in-Law took $5.3 million on Wednesday. Both trades noted that Black Friday is usually the holiday’s biggest moviegoing day, and THR said the East Coast storm could slow attendance.
stories.why: Thanksgiving is one of Hollywood’s biggest weekends, and the results shape what kinds of films studios bet on next: a franchise prequel looks safe, while a costly original animated film starting soft is a warning sign. Final weekend figures come on Sunday.

stories.headline: New York bans AI chatbot toys for five years, starting in February
stories.deck: Gov. Kathy Hochul signed a law on Tuesday, Nov. 24, putting a five-year moratorium on making, distributing and selling toys with built-in AI chatbots in New York. It takes effect 90 days after signing, so it does not cover this holiday season.
stories.summary: Gov. Kathy Hochul signed a law on Tuesday, Nov. 24, putting a five-year moratorium on making, distributing and selling toys with built-in AI chatbots in New York. It takes effect 90 days after signing, so it does not cover this holiday season. The law covers internet-connected talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots that hold conversations with children; the state attorney general can seek civil penalties of up to $15,000 a day per violation. Hochul’s office cited a consumer watchdog’s tests in which some chatbot toys discussed sexually explicit topics, told children where to find matches at home or acted upset when a child wanted to leave. NBC News reported that New York is the second state to ban such toys, after California. Hochul urged parents to weigh the risks before buying one as a gift.
stories.why: It is one of the first U.S. laws aimed squarely at AI products for young children, and other states may copy it. Because it starts in February, the toys can still be sold in New York this holiday season.
stories.label: Official statement + Reported
stories.note: Not covered in earlier editions; included because the ban targets holiday-season products.

stories.headline: After a fatal Toronto home invasion, Doug Ford tells Ontarians to “fight back” and says he would shoot an intruder
stories.deck: Ontario Premier Doug Ford said on Thursday, Nov. 26, that he is a legal gun owner and would use his gun against an armed intruder, and urged people without guns to use knives or baseball bats to protect their families. He spoke a day after musician Michael Eckert, 39, was shot dead in a home invasion in midtown Toronto.
stories.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford said on Thursday, Nov. 26, that he is a legal gun owner and would use his gun against an armed intruder, and urged people without guns to use knives or baseball bats to protect their families. He spoke a day after musician Michael Eckert, 39, was shot dead in a home invasion in midtown Toronto. “I encourage people to use whatever tool they have to fight back,” Ford told reporters at Queen’s Park, adding that he wants legal changes to address a spate of home invasions. Police say one or more suspects broke into a home on Poplar Plains Road near St. Clair Avenue West at about 2:30 a.m. on Wednesday; the killing came weeks after a home invasion in the Bridle Path area in which three residents were shot. Toronto police advised people facing intruders to call 911 first. NDP Leader Marit Stiles said Ford should focus on making people feel safe rather than telling them to arm themselves, and Green Leader Mike Schreiner called the advice “incredibly dangerous”.
stories.why: A premier openly encouraging people to use weapons on intruders is unusual in Canada, where self-defence law requires force to be reasonable and gun ownership is tightly regulated. Expect a debate over what legal changes Ford wants and whether his words could put people at risk.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement

stories.headline: Canada makes another advance payment on F-35 parts, keeping open the option of a 48-jet fleet while its review drags on
stories.deck: Ottawa has paid for more “long-lead” F-35 components, holding production slots that could bring Canada’s fleet to 48 jets, CBC News and The Globe and Mail reported on Nov. 26. The defence minister’s office says no decision has been made to buy more aircraft.
stories.summary: Ottawa has paid for more “long-lead” F-35 components, holding production slots that could bring Canada’s fleet to 48 jets, CBC News and The Globe and Mail reported on Nov. 26. The defence minister’s office says no decision has been made to buy more aircraft. Canada committed in 2023 to 88 F-35s, but Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered a review during the trade war with the U.S.; it is still unfinished about 20 months later, and Sweden’s Gripen is the competing option. Long-lead payments cover parts Lockheed Martin must order before assembly. A spokesperson for Defence Minister David McGuinty told CBC that “the proposed purchase of additional F-35s remains under review.” The Globe, citing officials it did not name, said the payments preserve Canada’s place in the production queue. Canada’s first two F-35s were recently delivered to Luke Air Force Base in Arizona, where Canadian crews are training.
stories.why: It is one of Canada’s biggest defence decisions and is tangled up with trade talks and U.S. pressure on Canadian defence spending. Paying to keep slots open lets Ottawa delay a choice without falling behind in the queue, but it also adds money to the F-35 side of the ledger.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement + Unnamed sources

stories.headline: Funeral-home boss sanctioned by the U.S. as an alleged mob figure was on police radar since 2019, CBC reports
stories.deck: Police records obtained by CBC News show Luigi Vescio Sr., president of a Toronto-area funeral-home chain that the U.S. sanctioned last week over alleged ’Ndrangheta ties, was photographed in 2019 meeting visitors described as leading Calabrian mafia figures.
stories.summary: Police records obtained by CBC News show Luigi Vescio Sr., president of a Toronto-area funeral-home chain that the U.S. sanctioned last week over alleged ’Ndrangheta ties, was photographed in 2019 meeting visitors described as leading Calabrian mafia figures. According to CBC, Ontario police captured the surveillance images and, months later, Italian authorities sought his arrest on a charge of mafia association. The U.S. Treasury on Nov. 19 named Vescio, 55, as a senior figure in the ’Ndrangheta’s Canadian wing and sanctioned his funeral homes and his wife and adult children. The Treasury has not said how the businesses are suspected of fitting into the alleged conspiracy. The allegations have not been tested in court.
stories.why: It adds detail to a rare U.S. move against alleged organized crime in Canada and sharpens a question already being asked: why Canadian law has not touched people whom U.S. and Italian authorities call mob leaders.

stories.headline: Shenzhen-bound ferry hits a floating dry dock off Tsing Yi, injuring at least 22
stories.deck: A high-speed ferry travelling from Sheung Wan to Shekou in Shenzhen crashed into dockyard facilities near the Tsing Yi oil depot on Friday morning, Nov. 27, Hong Kong time, injuring at least 22 people. RTHK said five were seriously hurt and all the injured were conscious.
stories.summary: A high-speed ferry travelling from Sheung Wan to Shekou in Shenzhen crashed into dockyard facilities near the Tsing Yi oil depot on Friday morning, Nov. 27, Hong Kong time, injuring at least 22 people. RTHK said five were seriously hurt and all the injured were conscious. Three of the seriously injured were taken to Princess Margaret Hospital and two to Yan Chai Hospital, according to RTHK. The Straits Times, citing the South China Morning Post, said the vessel, the Xin Xun Long Er Hao, had 35 passengers and 11 crew on board, and that a source said the captain lost control when the helm malfunctioned. Police are investigating. Reported injury figures differ: RTHK says 22, while the Straits Times headline and later reports say 24.
stories.why: Cross-boundary ferries between Hong Kong and Shenzhen carry many commuters and travellers, so the cause matters for safety checks across the fleet. The Straits Times says it is the second collision this year involving the operator’s parent company.

stories.headline: Licensed ride-hailing in Hong Kong slips into 2027 as vehicle-permit applications are pushed to early next year
stories.deck: Hong Kong’s Transport Department said on Nov. 26 that applications for the 10,000 ride-hailing vehicle permits will open in early 2027, with a ballot if demand exceeds the cap. Driver-permit applications open on Nov. 30, with no quota.
stories.summary: Hong Kong’s Transport Department said on Nov. 26 that applications for the 10,000 ride-hailing vehicle permits will open in early 2027, with a ballot if demand exceeds the cap. Driver-permit applications open on Nov. 30, with no quota. The Standard reported that the timing means licensed platforms will not start operating before the end of 2026, later than the original target, with sources citing the time needed to vet up to eight platform applications. Driver permits require applicants to be at least 21, to have held a full licence for a year, to pass the combined taxi and ride-hailing written test and to complete a pre-service course; taxi licence holders can apply directly. The Standard said the vehicle-permit ballot will give extra chances to people who have already passed the test or hold a driving permit, and to people who owned a private car before Aug. 3, 2026, to discourage a rush to buy cars.
stories.why: This is the city’s first attempt to legalise services like Uber, which have run in a grey area for years. The delay and the ballot rules decide who can drive legally and when riders get licensed options.

stories.headline: Couple arrested after Hong Kong says ‘missing’ passport pages behind a viral complaint were torn out
stories.deck: Hong Kong’s Immigration Department arrested a 27-year-old woman and her 34-year-old boyfriend on Thursday evening, Nov. 26 (Hong Kong time), after government lab tests showed four pages missing from her passport had been ripped out. She had claimed online that a printing defect led Japan to refuse her entry.
stories.summary: Hong Kong’s Immigration Department arrested a 27-year-old woman and her 34-year-old boyfriend on Thursday evening, Nov. 26 (Hong Kong time), after government lab tests showed four pages missing from her passport had been ripped out. She had claimed online that a printing defect led Japan to refuse her entry. Chief Immigration Officer Tang Wai-yip said the Government Laboratory found paper-fibre residue where pages 15 to 18 were missing, The Standard reported. The pair were arrested in Lam Tin on suspicion of altering a travel document without lawful authority, possessing and using an altered travel document, and misleading immigration officers. Officials said the passport was issued in 2018 and had been used for several trips without problems. The two have been arrested, not charged.

stories.headline: Satellite images show China’s military building floating bridges from civilian ships in landing drills near Taiwan, Reuters reports

A senior security official said the drill was still under way on Friday.

A senior security official said the drill was still under way on Friday. The activity, first spotted on Nov. 1 about 280 km from Taiwan’s main island, involved eight civilian vessels plus landing craft and nearby navy ships, according to the geospatial firm ingeniSPACE; no purpose-built bridging equipment was seen. The official, who was not named, said the drill was meant to “practice the swift seizure of small islands” and was aimed at contingencies along the first island chain. China’s defence ministry did not respond to Reuters, but it said on Thursday, when asked about recent drills, that its training was “entirely legitimate and reasonable”. Taiwan’s defence ministry said it was aware of the activity. The report came on the eve of Taiwan’s local elections on Saturday, Nov. 28; the official made no direct link between the two.
stories.why: Getting troops and heavy equipment ashore is one of the hardest parts of any invasion, and using civilian ships suggests China could improvise landing points along Taiwan’s coast. It is a rehearsal, not an attack, but Taiwan, the U.S. and Japan watch it closely.

Changing the name appears to be a key condition for Lithuania restoring normal relations with Beijing. The office opened in 2021 as the first in Europe to use “Taiwanese” instead of the customary “Taipei”; China responded by downgrading diplomatic ties and restricting trade. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius told the ELTA news agency on Wednesday that the office’s accreditation, granted by ministerial order, could be revoked if Taiwan refused to change the name — “We would not want that, but this option could be used” — and President Gitanas Nausėda made similar remarks. On Thursday Sinkevičius said withdrawing accreditation was not the government’s objective, and MP Motuzas told LRT there was no plan to close the office. Taiwan’s ministry called for “good faith and mutual respect”.
stories.why: Lithuania became a symbol of standing up to Beijing in 2021 and paid for it in trade. A reversal would show how China’s economic pressure can work on smaller countries, and other European governments weighing ties with Taiwan will be watching.

About 738,000 people moved to the UK for a year or more and 661,000 left, the BBC reported from the figures, a 92% fall in net migration from the record 944,000 in the year to March 2023. stories.dateLabel: Proposed Nov 25, 2026; reactions Nov 25–26 (update to the Nov 25 edition)
stories.headline: U.S. proposes new tariffs on 14 economies, including China, the EU and Japan; Beijing says it “reserves the right” to respond
stories.deck: The U.S. Trade Representative on Wednesday, Nov. 25, proposed new tariffs on goods from 14 economies it says fuel “structural excess capacity”, with proposed ceilings ranging from 15% to 35% depending on the country. The duties are proposals: public comments are due Jan. 5 and hearings start Jan. 25, 2027.
stories.summary: The U.S. Trade Representative on Wednesday, Nov. 25, proposed new tariffs on goods from 14 economies it says fuel “structural excess capacity”, with proposed ceilings ranging from 15% to 35% depending on the country. The duties are proposals: public comments are due Jan. 5 and hearings start Jan. 25, 2027. The 14 are China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, South Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan and India; the USTR made no finding on Mexico or Norway. According to the USTR’s release, the proposed ceilings include up to 15% for the EU, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan, up to 18% for several Southeast Asian countries and Bangladesh, up to 20% for most Chinese goods and Singapore, up to 25% for India and up to 35% for Vietnam, in each case adjusted for existing deals and duties. Reports differ on the effective rate for China: the USTR release lists up to 20% for most goods, AFP says the rate could double to 40%, and the Guardian says stacking on other duties could take some goods to 45%. China’s commerce ministry said on Thursday that “overcapacity” was a “pretext for protectionism” and that China “reserves the right to take necessary measures”; Japan called the move “regrettable” and Singapore said it was “very disappointed”. Brazil, which faces a separate proposal, said it “will not yield to this type of threat”. The USTR’s Jamieson Greer said the plan would “level the playing field for American workers”.
stories.why: Tariffs are paid by importers and often passed on in prices, so if these go ahead in 2027 they could show up in the cost of electronics, clothes and other everyday goods. For now it is a proposal with a comment period, which is why trading partners are reacting with words rather than retaliation. The China rate matters most: the current U.S.–China truce runs to Jan. 10, just before the hearings.
stories.label: Official statement + Reported
stories.note: Follows the Nov 25 edition, which reported the BBC’s account that tariffs were being prepared; the USTR has now published the proposals. Reactions from China, Japan and Singapore are from RTHK and France 24 (AFP/Reuters copy).

stories.deck: Macy’s has moved its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade from Thursday, Nov. 26, to Saturday, Nov. 28, because of forecast heavy rain and strong winds, the first weather postponement in the parade’s history, according to the BBC.
stories.summary: Macy’s has moved its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade from Thursday, Nov. 26, to Saturday, Nov. 28, because of forecast heavy rain and strong winds, the first weather postponement in the parade’s history, according to the BBC. The decision was announced on Wednesday, Nov. 25, while balloons were already being inflated; executive producer Will Cross said they would be deflated and stored in New Jersey until Saturday. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said “extreme weather has forced” the change. Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency for New York City, Long Island and Westchester, and New Jersey declared one statewide. The National Weather Service issued a high wind warning for the city from 10 a.m. Thursday to 1 a.m. Friday, with gusts possibly reaching 60 mph. NBC said it would air the 2025 parade on Thursday. Nationally, NPR reports hundreds of flights already cancelled or delayed by early Thursday as storms hit both coasts, with AAA expecting 81.5 million people to travel between Thursday and Monday. Balloons were grounded once before, in 1971, and the parade was cancelled outright in 1942–44.
stories.why: For New Yorkers this changes Thanksgiving plans: the march down from the Upper West Side to Herald Square moves to the weekend, and Thursday itself is a storm day with official warnings to stay off the roads. It is also a rare break in a century-old tradition, and whether every performer returns on Saturday is still unclear.

stories.note: The parade is planned for Saturday, Nov. 28; whether all performers and celebrities scheduled for Thursday will take part is unclear, the BBC says.

stories.headline: Army detonates Iowa lead azide stockpile and calls it a “huge success”; EPA says early air monitoring found no airborne lead
stories.deck: The U.S. Army detonated its stockpile of the explosive lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant at about 10 a.m. ET on Wednesday, Nov. 25, after weeks of delays, public alarm and legal challenges.
stories.summary: The U.S. Army detonated its stockpile of the explosive lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant at about 10 a.m. ET on Wednesday, Nov. 25, after weeks of delays, public alarm and legal challenges. Smoke rose over the area near Middletown before dispersing, and an all-clear was issued. The Army called the operation a “huge success”. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said late Wednesday that air monitors were detecting zero airborne lead, that more than 1,000 samples had been taken from homes, parks, farms and taps, and that laboratory results were expected over the following 24 to 48 hours, with churches, schools and playgrounds to be sampled on Thursday. Figures for the amount differ slightly: the Guardian says 9,700 lb (4,400 kg), the BBC “nearly five tonnes”. Some residents had feared a toxic plume; one Burlington resident told the AP the blast was smaller than expected.
stories.why: This closes the most anxious chapter of a story that had residents across a 100-mile radius preparing to shelter in place. The “success” claim rests on early readings from the Army and the EPA; independent lab results due over the next two days are what will actually show whether soil and water were affected.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement
stories.note: Earlier editions (Nov 23–25) reported the detonation as planned; it has now taken place. The safety findings are the Army’s and EPA’s own early statements; lab results were still pending.

stories.headline: Supreme Court of Canada to rule Friday on Quebec’s religious-symbols law and the notwithstanding clause
stories.deck: The Supreme Court of Canada says it will release its decision on Quebec’s secularism law, Bill 21, at 9:45 a.m. ET on Friday, Nov. 27, CBC reports.
stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada says it will release its decision on Quebec’s secularism law, Bill 21, at 9:45 a.m. ET on Friday, Nov. 27, CBC reports. The 2019 law bars some public sector workers, including teachers and police officers, from wearing religious symbols on the job. It was shielded with the Constitution’s notwithstanding clause, which lets governments override certain Charter rights for renewable five-year periods, and the big question is whether the court will set limits on that power. Legal observers quoted by CBC expect the ruling to matter well beyond Quebec; the court is already scheduled to hear a Saskatchewan notwithstanding-clause case on school pronoun rules in March. The Parti Québécois, which now leads a minority government, has vowed to go further than Bill 21.
stories.why: The notwithstanding clause is increasingly used by provinces to shield laws from court challenges, so the decision could reshape how far any Canadian government can go in overriding rights. Until Friday morning, though, nothing has been decided.

stories.headline: Hongkongers lay flowers for the 168 Tai Po fire victims on the first anniversary, as some lament the lack of an official memorial
stories.deck: Mourners left flowers, notes and paper cranes at a park beside Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po on Thursday, Nov. 26, one year after the fire that killed 168 people, while some told Hong Kong Free Press they were disappointed the government held no official remembrance.
stories.summary: Mourners left flowers, notes and paper cranes at a park beside Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po on Thursday, Nov. 26, one year after the fire that killed 168 people, while some told Hong Kong Free Press they were disappointed the government held no official remembrance. A makeshift altar grew through the morning at the Kwong Fuk Sitting-out Area as plainclothes officers watched, HKFP reported; RTHK said former residents observed a moment of silence. Chief Secretary Eric Chan said on Tuesday that the government would not host official mourning events and urged people to be “careful” about which memorials they joined; one mourner told HKFP that a government-organised event was “the least authorities could do.” Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong said on Thursday that support for displaced residents would continue: most of the almost 2,000 households have agreed to sell their flats to the government, about 1,400 have chosen subsidised flats, and legislation to take the remaining units would be a “last resort” and not before next year. An independent committee’s report last month found the blaze, which spread during a renovation, was preventable and that government departments mishandled residents’ complaints.
stories.why: A year on, the anniversary shows two Hong Kongs side by side: grief expressed quietly at a roadside altar, and an official approach that offers money and rehousing but avoids public mourning. With police enquiries around memorial events already defended by the security chief this week, how people are allowed to remember is itself part of the story.

stories.headline: British lawyer says China misuses Interpol red notices to target dissidents, days before Hong Kong hosts Interpol’s assembly
stories.deck: A British lawyer who specialises in Interpol “red notices” told the Guardian that China is misusing the system to target and silence dissidents abroad, ahead of Interpol’s 94th general assembly in Hong Kong from Nov. 30 to Dec. 3.
stories.summary: A British lawyer who specialises in Interpol “red notices” told the Guardian that China is misusing the system to target and silence dissidents abroad, ahead of Interpol’s 94th general assembly in Hong Kong from Nov. 30 to Dec. 3. Ben Keith said he was working on five cases involving questionable Chinese requests, and that he had asked Interpol in July whether Beijing had sought notices against five prominent UK-based Chinese dissidents without a substantive answer. A report he co-wrote, “The Red Notice Trap”, cites the case of Uyghur activist Idris Hasan, held in Morocco for nearly four years on a Chinese red notice that Interpol itself suspended within two weeks. stories.summary: Kilmar Ábrego García, the Maryland man wrongly deported to a Salvadoran prison in 2025, left the United States for Spain on a commercial flight on Tuesday, Nov. 24, his lawyers and U.S. officials said. The government had admitted he was sent to El Salvador by mistake despite a 2019 court order protecting him; he was brought back in June 2025 to face human-smuggling charges that were later dismissed, and officials then tried to send him to countries including Uganda, Ghana and Liberia. The Guardian, citing the Washington Post, reported that he negotiated a deal to leave voluntarily rather than be forcibly removed. His lawyer called it a “temporary departure” and said they expect a future administration to let him return to his U.S.-citizen wife and child. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote on X that Ábrego García had “self-deported” and repeated accusations, without evidence, that he was a gang member and trafficker. stories.why: This case became the best-known test of whether the government must follow court orders and give due process before deporting someone. stories.deck: Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem said on Tuesday, Nov. 24, that a “second-round effect” of the 2026 oil shock will keep inflation elevated in 2027, as businesses pass more of their higher energy and transport costs on to consumers.
stories.summary: Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem said on Tuesday, Nov. 24, that a “second-round effect” of the 2026 oil shock will keep inflation elevated in 2027, as businesses pass more of their higher energy and transport costs on to consumers. Speaking to the Economic Club of Canada in Toronto, he said “this second-round effect of the oil shock will add to inflation persistence” and that the bank is preparing for “larger and more frequent supply shocks.” Canada’s inflation rate was 3.1% in October, and the bank raised its policy rate by a quarter point to 2.5% in October. CIBC chief economist Avery Shenfeld wrote that the remarks point to another hike at the bank’s Dec. 9 decision rather than in January. In the same speech Macklem published the conclusions of the bank’s five-year review, which kept the 2% inflation target, and launched a new inflation dashboard. Macklem announced earlier in November that he will step down when his term ends on June 2, 2027.
stories.why: For anyone with a variable-rate loan, a line of credit or a lease coming up, this is a signal that borrowing costs may rise again before they fall. Macklem is also saying that cheaper oil now will not quickly show up in other prices.

stories.headline: On the eve of the Tai Po fire anniversary, Hong Kong’s security chief defends police checks on memorial events, citing “sedition” risks
stories.deck: Security Secretary Chris Tang said on Wednesday, Nov. 25, that police enquiries into memorial events ahead of the first anniversary of the Wang Fuk Court fire were needed to assess risks and stop people “using the special date to conduct seditious acts.”
stories.summary: Security Secretary Chris Tang said on Wednesday, Nov. 25, that police enquiries into memorial events ahead of the first anniversary of the Wang Fuk Court fire were needed to assess risks and stop people “using the special date to conduct seditious acts.” The blaze in Tai Po on Nov. 26, 2025, killed 168 people. Earlier in November police made enquiries with two Catholic churches planning memorial services; one, in Tai Po, replaced its anniversary mass with a general service, and parishioners suggested that followed official pressure. Tang said lawful memorials are allowed but some people might try to “hijack” them, and that the government does not count how many events have been called off. Beijing’s Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office and its liaison office in the city both published commentaries on Tuesday praising the city government’s “strong resolve” and reforms after the fire. RTHK reported that Chief Executive John Lee visited displaced residents who will move into new homes, and the government said households will get two more rental subsidy payments of HK$75,000 each, in December and June 2027.
stories.why: A year on, the government is presenting the fire as a story of relief and reform, while treating unofficial remembrance as a possible security risk. How Thursday’s private memorials go will show how much room is left for public grief that the authorities do not organise.

stories.headline: Brooklyn jury convicts Huawei of stealing U.S. trade secrets and bank fraud but acquits it of racketeering; Beijing condemns “suppression”
stories.deck: A federal jury in Brooklyn on Tuesday, Nov. 24, found Huawei guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank fraud and conspiracy to violate U.S. sanctions on Iran, but acquitted the Chinese tech giant of the central racketeering charge.
stories.summary: A federal jury in Brooklyn on Tuesday, Nov. 24, found Huawei guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank fraud and conspiracy to violate U.S. sanctions on Iran, but acquitted the Chinese tech giant of the central racketeering charge. The racketeering count would have required jurors to find that Huawei acted as a criminal enterprise; it was also cleared of obstruction of justice, according to AFP. Prosecutors had accused Huawei and three subsidiaries of spending two decades lying to banks about its business in Iran and stealing technology from rivals. “No person or company is above the law,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said. Huawei said the acquittal “confirms that these allegations lack factual basis” and called the remaining convictions “without legal or factual merit”, promising “all necessary legal actions”. Its lawyer told the BBC he expects an appeal. Sentencing is planned for September 2027. China’s foreign ministry said on Wednesday it “firmly opposes the US suppressing and containing Chinese enterprises.” The case dates to 2018, when Huawei finance chief Meng Wanzhou was arrested in Canada, setting off a three-way diplomatic crisis.
stories.why: This is the most significant U.S. criminal verdict yet against a major Chinese tech company, and it lands a week after the Trump–Xi summit and alongside reports of new U.S. tariffs. A conviction adds legal weight to Washington’s long-running case against Huawei’s equipment. Experts quoted by the Guardian say the case has not undermined Huawei’s business, though, so the bigger effects may be diplomatic rather than commercial.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement + Allegation
stories.note: Huawei can appeal; convictions are not final until sentencing and any appeals. Sources differ on trial length (“two-month” per the BBC; “more than two months” per the Guardian; “three-month” per AFP via HKFP).

stories.headline: China investigates Shanghai party chief Chen Jining, the fourth Politburo member to be targeted since 2025
stories.deck: China’s anti-corruption watchdog is investigating Shanghai Communist Party secretary Chen Jining, a member of the 24-member Politburo, for “suspected severe violations of discipline and laws”, Chinese state media announced on Tuesday, Nov. 24.
stories.summary: China’s anti-corruption watchdog is investigating Shanghai Communist Party secretary Chen Jining, a member of the 24-member Politburo, for “suspected severe violations of discipline and laws”, Chinese state media announced on Tuesday, Nov. 24. The phrase is a common euphemism for corruption, and a public announcement of this kind usually signals an official’s downfall. Chen, 62, an environmental scientist with a doctorate from Imperial College London, was president of Tsinghua University, then environment minister from 2015, mayor of Beijing and, from 2022, party chief of Shanghai. He is the fourth Politburo member from the body formed in 2022 to be investigated, after He Weidong, Zhang Youxia and Ma Xingrui. The Shanghai party committee said it “expressed firm support” for the decision. The Guardian reported that a Weibo hashtag on the case had about 240 million views by Wednesday morning, with many users saying they were shocked.
stories.why: Chen was widely seen as a rising star and possible candidate for higher office, so his fall suggests that no one in Xi Jinping’s leadership is safe from the anti-corruption campaign. Purges at this level also reshape who could rise to the very top of China’s leadership.
stories.label: Reported + State media + Analysis

stories.summary: Police in China contacted at least three members of a WeChat group, or their parents, after the group discussed attending a Melbourne vigil for Feng Jianming, a HungryPanda delivery rider allegedly murdered on Nov. 6, Guardian Australia reported. The group, which grew to more than 400 members, was disbanded after the calls; members declined to speak on the record, citing safety concerns. Australia’s Home Affairs department said it is “unacceptable for any foreign government to target members of our community”. The Chinese embassy in Canberra declined to comment.
stories.why: If chats on a Chinese-owned app can lead to calls from police back home, Chinese workers and students abroad may stay silent even about local issues like pay and safety. stories.deck: Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale signed a treaty in Canberra on Wednesday, Nov. 25, making Australia the Pacific nation’s “security partner of choice”, after reports that Honiara told Beijing it would not renew a controversial 2022 security pact.
stories.summary: Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale signed a treaty in Canberra on Wednesday, Nov. 25, making Australia the Pacific nation’s “security partner of choice”, after reports that Honiara told Beijing it would not renew a controversial 2022 security pact. The Guardian reports the deal includes A$740 million in Australian funding over 10 years, mostly grants, and commits Solomon Islands not to host foreign military bases or major security infrastructure. About 14 Chinese police officers posted under the old pact are expected to leave by the middle of 2027; the BBC says the China pact was understood to expire in April 2027. “Solomon Islands has been, for a number of years, a source of uncertainty and doubt in the region… Those days are done. Gone,” Wale said. He said there were “ongoing discussions” with China but that he could not discuss the pact because of a non-disclosure agreement. China’s foreign ministry did not confirm or deny that the pact had been ended, saying its co-operation involves no “geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation”.
stories.why: The 2022 pact was the biggest sign of China’s growing security reach in the South Pacific, so its end is a significant reversal in the U.S.–China–Australia contest for influence there. It also shows how much small island states can gain by being courted by both sides.
stories.label: Official statement + Reported
stories.note: The termination of the China pact is reported by Australian media and the Guardian; Beijing had not confirmed it. The Guardian’s “$740m” is assumed to be Australian dollars.

stories.headline: Leaked Russian death records show at least 490,000 soldiers killed in the Ukraine war, BBC and independent Russian outlets find
stories.deck: Leaked records from Russia’s own statistics agency show at least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022, according to an analysis by BBC Russian published on Tuesday, Nov. 24.
stories.summary: Leaked records from Russia’s own statistics agency show at least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022, according to an analysis by BBC Russian published on Tuesday, Nov. 24. The more than 11 million death records, from 2021 to September 2026, were taken in a hack by the Belarusian group Cyber Partisans and Ukraine’s Silent Crow. Rosstat acknowledged a cyber-attack but denied that protected information leaked. The BBC says the data matched 90% of its own open-source list of confirmed deaths. In the records, 65% of Russians aged 18 to 24 who died in 2025 were killed in the war, and men from poor Siberian regions such as Tyva and Buryatia were 20 to 25 times more likely to die in it than residents of Moscow or St Petersburg. Independent Russian outlets Meduza and Mediazona, analysing the same data, also count about 490,000 registered deaths and estimate more than 700,000 once missing soldiers are included, with wide uncertainty for the past year.
stories.why: Russia does not publish its war dead, so these figures are the closest view yet of the human cost from its own records. They show the burden falling hardest on young men and poorer regions, which matters for how long Russia can keep fighting and for any peace talks.
stories.label: Reported + Analysis
stories.note: Based on hacked data whose authenticity the BBC, Meduza and Mediazona say they tested; Rosstat denies protected information leaked. Figures are lower bounds for registered deaths; the 700,000 figure is Meduza and Mediazona’s estimate. Meduza is an independent Russian outlet based outside Russia.

stories.summary: Colombian police and soldiers stormed a supermarket in the Caribbean city of Cartagena shortly after midnight on Wednesday, Nov. 25, freeing about 20 shoppers and employees held at gunpoint for roughly 17 hours, President Abelardo de la Espriella said. Gunmen had entered the Éxito store at about 8 a.m. on Tuesday after what local media described as a failed attempt to rob an armoured car, and then demanded safe passage out. They released about 10 hostages during the day, including elderly women. Security forces used stun grenades as they went in, and one hostage-taker was killed. Cartagena’s mayor said all the hostages were “safe and sound”.

stories.headline: Sport’s top court gives the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations title back to Senegal; Morocco plans to challenge
stories.deck: The Court of Arbitration for Sport on Tuesday, Nov. 24, reinstated Senegal as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations champions, overturning a ruling that had handed the title to hosts Morocco after Senegal’s players walked off during the final.
stories.summary: The Court of Arbitration for Sport on Tuesday, Nov. 24, reinstated Senegal as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations champions, overturning a ruling that had handed the title to hosts Morocco after Senegal’s players walked off during the final. In January’s final in Rabat, Senegal left the pitch in second-half stoppage time to protest a penalty awarded to Morocco; play resumed after more than 15 minutes, Brahim Díaz’s spot kick was saved, and Senegal won 1-0 in extra time through Pape Gueye. A Confederation of African Football appeals board later awarded Morocco a 3-0 default win. The three CAS judges ruled unanimously that the referee, Jean-Jacques Ndala, “did not err in law” and had sole authority to restart the match. Morocco plans to appeal, likely to Switzerland’s supreme court, challenging the integrity of a senior CAS judge, NPR reported; Senegal’s lawyer called the allegation “unreal”.
stories.why: The ruling settles, for now, a 10-month fight over who won Africa’s biggest football tournament, and it backs the referee’s authority over what happens on the pitch. A Swiss appeal is possible only on narrow procedural grounds, so Senegal is likely, though not certain, to keep the title.

stories.note: Morocco’s challenge to a CAS judge’s integrity is an allegation and had not been decided when this edition was prepared.

stories.why: Edochie helped shape the style of Nollywood, now one of the world’s largest film industries, and his Okonkwo brought Achebe’s classic novel to a huge television audience.

stories.headline: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO after Trump says he “convinced” the board, and Congress lines up questions
stories.deck: Nvidia’s board gave Jensen Huang his job back on Monday, Nov. 23, less than two weeks after he resigned over an affair with a woman some U.S. intelligence officials allege was a Chinese spy. President Trump says he persuaded the board.
stories.summary: Nvidia’s board gave Jensen Huang his job back on Monday, Nov. 23, less than two weeks after he resigned over an affair with a woman some U.S. intelligence officials allege was a Chinese spy. President Trump says he persuaded the board. Huang, the chipmaker’s co-founder, stepped down on Nov. 12 after admitting the relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), a businesswoman tied to the Singapore-based data-centre firm Megaspeed; China calls the spying accusations groundless. Only last week the board had said it did not plan to bring him back. On Monday chairman Harvey Jones said the reinstatement was in the “best interests” of shareholders, staff and partners, and the board said input from senior U.S. officials left it confident Huang posed no national-security risk. Trump told CNBC: “I spoke to them… And I convinced them.” He said Attorney General Todd Blanche had confirmed the government has no evidence Huang broke the law. Nvidia shares jumped about 31%, adding close to $1 trillion in market value and lifting the Nasdaq 6.5%, though the stock was still about 21% below its level a month ago, the BBC reported. Also on Monday, the Commerce Department said it plans to put Megaspeed on its trade blacklist. Huang is scheduled to face the Senate banking committee on Dec. 3 and to give transcribed interviews to several House committees. Democratic senator Chris Van Hollen called the reinstatement “exhibit A” of “political corruption”, and lawmakers from both parties are expected to press Huang on his China ties.
stories.why: This is about more than one CEO. A president personally steering who runs America’s most valuable chip company, while vouching for that person on national security, mixes politics, markets and intelligence in an unusual way. Nvidia’s chips power the AI boom, so its leadership moves retirement savings and the wider stock market. Next week’s congressional hearings are the first public test of what the government actually knows.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement + Allegation
stories.note: Updates the Nov 23 edition, which reported a (Reuters, unconfirmed by the BBC) SEC inquiry into Nvidia’s accounting. That inquiry is still reported only by outlets citing unnamed sources. The spying accusation against Alice Huang comes from intelligence reports described to journalists, not from charges; China denies it. Hearing dates are scheduled, not yet held.

stories.headline: Appeals court clears the Army to detonate unstable explosives in Iowa, now planned for Wednesday morning
stories.deck: A federal appeals court on Monday, Nov. 23, let the Army go ahead with blowing up 68 drums of degraded lead azide at a plant in Middletown, Iowa, hours after President Trump had ordered a pause.
stories.summary: A federal appeals court on Monday, Nov. 23, let the Army go ahead with blowing up 68 drums of degraded lead azide at a plant in Middletown, Iowa, hours after President Trump had ordered a pause. The 8th Circuit found there was an emergency reason and adequate safeguards, the BBC reported. Army Secretary Adam Telle then said the controlled detonation of the material, nearly 9,500 lb (about five tonnes), will take place on Wednesday morning, Nov. 25, calling it a “consensus decision”. Earlier on Monday Trump had written that he would not proceed unless the courts and Iowa’s Democratic governor-elect, Rob Sand, agreed, and that he would hold Sand responsible “for any and all death or destruction” if not. Sand, who takes office in January, asked the federal government to share more information with the public. The Environmental Protection Agency granted an emergency permit, saying the risk of the chemical exploding on its own was an imminent threat. The Army has warned that a plume of lead dust could reach up to 100 miles. Middletown, home to about 400 people, has a mayor who backs the detonation.
stories.why: This is a choice between two risks: leaving an unstable explosive in place or setting it off on purpose and managing the dust. Trump’s attempt to shift responsibility onto a governor who hasn’t taken office yet turned a safety decision into a political one. Whether Wednesday’s blast goes as planned, and what monitoring shows afterwards, will matter to towns downwind in Iowa and Illinois.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement + Claim
stories.note: Updates the Nov 23 edition, which reported the Army’s plan despite a lower-court pause. The detonation is scheduled, not confirmed, as of this edition. The 100-mile plume figure is the Army’s own warning as reported by the Guardian.

stories.deck: California Democrat Jimmy Gomez said on Monday, Nov. 23, he will leave Congress on Dec. 1, after a bipartisan House Ethics Committee report found substantial evidence he made unwelcome sexual advances toward a House staffer.
stories.summary: California Democrat Jimmy Gomez said on Monday, Nov. 23, he will leave Congress on Dec. 1, after a bipartisan House Ethics Committee report found substantial evidence he made unwelcome sexual advances toward a House staffer. Gomez said he cooperated but has “strong disagreements” with the report, which he says leaves out key parts of his testimony, while taking responsibility for “personal mistakes” outside his marriage. He had already lost his November re-election race to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres and was due to leave in January. Lawyers for the staffer, who is not named, said she testified at personal risk. House Democratic leaders Hakeem Jeffries, Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar called the report “serious and deeply troubling” and backed reforming House rules on harassment.
stories.why: Gomez was leaving anyway, so the resignation changes little in the House count. The bigger story is the incoming Democratic majority promising new rules to protect staff, which will be an early test of whether Congress polices its own members. The report’s findings are the committee’s conclusions, not a criminal verdict.

stories.deck: From Jan. 19, 2027, Citi Bike members will pay no more than $3.65 for an e-bike ride of up to 45 minutes, under a deal Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced with Lyft on Monday, Nov. 23.
stories.summary: From Jan. 19, 2027, Citi Bike members will pay no more than $3.65 for an e-bike ride of up to 45 minutes, under a deal Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced with Lyft on Monday, Nov. 23. Members now pay 27 cents a minute on e-bikes, or $12.15 for a 45-minute ride, except trips into or out of Manhattan, which are capped at $5.40; the new cap replaces that one. The annual membership fee ($239) and member per-minute and overage fees are frozen immediately until May 26, 2029, when Lyft’s contract with the city ends, the mayor’s office said. Riders in the Reduced Fare Bike Share program are covered too. In return the city will make it easier to install charging at more than 130 stations from early 2027, let Lyft sell ads on station panels from Jan. 1, and change revenue sharing so Lyft pays the city only above a $5.25 million yearly threshold. Prices for non-members are not covered by the agreement, Gothamist reported. Mamdani said the cap would have saved riders about $11 million last year.
stories.why: For anyone who bikes to class or work, a long e-bike ride drops from about $12 to under $4, which makes Citi Bike a real alternative to the subway for some trips. The city pays nothing directly; it gives up ad space and revenue instead. The catch is the price freeze ends in 2029, when the contract is renegotiated.

stories.headline: Pentagon “fact sheet” accuses Canada of low military readiness and of putting “parochial” economic interests ahead of defence
stories.deck: A U.S. Department of War document posted on Monday, Nov. 23, says Canada is not meeting its NORAD or NATO obligations and has no funded plan to reach NATO’s 5% defence-spending target by 2035.
stories.summary: A U.S. Department of War document posted on Monday, Nov. 23, says Canada is not meeting its NORAD or NATO obligations and has no funded plan to reach NATO’s 5% defence-spending target by 2035. The fact sheet, first reported by Axios on Sunday, says only 41.9% of the Royal Canadian Air Force’s fleet is ready for operations this budget year, cites low army and navy readiness and notes that just one of Canada’s four Victoria-class submarines is seaworthy at a time. It accuses Ottawa of prioritising “parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization”, which it says will “further burden… the American taxpayer”, and points to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s ongoing review of the F-35 purchase. It also says Canada is deferring the biggest spending increases until after the 2029 federal election. The draft would exempt Alto from the whole Expropriation Act and from parts of the Railway Safety Act, the Impact Assessment Act and railway crossing rules. Crossing disputes for farms and roads split by the line would go to private arbitration, with costs shared up to $25,000 per party. stories.deck: Ahead of the first anniversary of the Wang Fuk Court fire on Nov. 26, the Hong Kong government said on Tuesday, Nov. 24 (Hong Kong time), that it will not host official memorial events, and announced two new grants for victims worth about HK$630 million.
stories.summary: Ahead of the first anniversary of the Wang Fuk Court fire on Nov. 26, the Hong Kong government said on Tuesday, Nov. 24 (Hong Kong time), that it will not host official memorial events, and announced two new grants for victims worth about HK$630 million. Chief Secretary Eric Chan told Commercial Radio that many community and religious memorials are already planned, that the government would not obstruct lawful ones and might help with transport, but urged people to choose “carefully” because some online were trying to use memorials to “make trouble”, Hong Kong Free Press reported. Under the new “New Beginning” grants, each flat owner gets HK$300,000 in two instalments (end of December 2026 and end of June 2027), and the family of each person who died gets HK$200,000 in December, paid through social workers without applications. Families of foreign domestic helpers who died will be contacted through consulates. Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak said the HK$4.5 billion support fund is now largely used up. The fire spread across seven blocks of the estate in Tai Po during renovation work in November 2025, killing 168 people.

The “safeguard” quotas, announced in the EU’s Official Journal, apply for up to 200 days while an investigation into hybrid and plug-in hybrid imports continues; over that period China’s share works out to about 191,000 cars, the Guardian reported. Under trade rules the caps must cover all big exporters, so Japan, Turkey, South Korea, the U.K. and others also get quotas, but most are set high enough to cover their current shipments, Reuters reported. The EU says China’s hybrid exports worldwide jumped from 191,000 in 2023 to 1.124 million in 2025, as Chinese makers shifted to hybrids after the EU put tariffs on fully electric cars in 2024. stories.why: Chinese carmakers found a way around EU tariffs on electric cars by shipping hybrids, and Europe is now closing that gap to protect its own car industry and jobs. stories.headline: South Korea sounds a brief air-raid alert on Ulleung Island as Russian military planes approach its airspace
stories.deck: Residents of South Korea’s Ulleung Island were told to take shelter on Tuesday morning, Nov. 24, local time, after about five Russian military aircraft entered South Korea’s air defence zone and came close to the island’s airspace, the military said.
stories.summary: Residents of South Korea’s Ulleung Island were told to take shelter on Tuesday morning, Nov. 24, local time, after about five Russian military aircraft entered South Korea’s air defence zone and came close to the island’s airspace, the military said. The interior ministry sent an “EVACUATION, AIR RAID” text at 7:52 a.m. and lifted it three minutes later; sirens sounded and TV broadcasts carried warnings. South Korean fighters were scrambled and the Russian planes left without entering the airspace, the Joint Chiefs of Staff said, adding that the alert was issued pre-emptively because a violation was anticipated. A provincial alert first wrongly said the planes were suspected to be North Korean, before being corrected, Al Jazeera reported. The defence ministry said it would summon Russia’s defence attaché to protest. Ulleung, a volcanic island of about 9,000 people, lies roughly 120 km off the east coast.
stories.why: An air-raid alert for a real island, even for three minutes, shows how quickly a military flight can turn into civilian panic, especially after the confusing North Korea mix-up. Seoul’s formal protest to Moscow is the next step to watch.

stories.headline: Australia’s online safety bill, set to pass with Greens support, would let people sue platforms and fine them up to 5% of global revenue
stories.deck: Australia’s Labor government struck a deal with the Greens on Tuesday, Nov. 24, to pass a “digital duty of care” law that would expose social media and tech firms to fines of up to 5% of their worldwide revenue and give individuals a right to sue.
stories.summary: Australia’s Labor government struck a deal with the Greens on Tuesday, Nov. 24, to pass a “digital duty of care” law that would expose social media and tech firms to fines of up to 5% of their worldwide revenue and give individuals a right to sue. The bill would replace a patchwork of industry codes with one legal duty on social media, games, apps, search and AI chatbots to provide a safe online environment, targeting harms such as child sexual abuse material, fake nude images, self-harm promotion and terrorism. From late 2027 Australians aged 16 and over would be able to switch off algorithm-driven feeds, and “endless scroll” features may be curbed. The maximum fine had previously been proposed at A$109 million, Al Jazeera reported. Communications Minister Anika Wells said she had met the U.S. ambassador about the laws and dared firms to challenge them: “bring it on.” The opposition Coalition opposed the bill, citing free-speech concerns. The government expects it to pass parliament this week.
stories.why: Australia already banned social media for under-16s; this goes further by making platforms legally responsible for harm to everyone and letting users take them to court. Other governments watch Australia’s tech laws closely, and the minister’s meeting with the U.S. ambassador shows Washington is paying attention too.

stories.headline: Molly Meldrum, the Countdown host who shaped decades of Australian pop, dies at 83
stories.deck: Ian “Molly” Meldrum, the broadcaster and music journalist who hosted the ABC’s Countdown and championed acts from INXS to Kylie Minogue, died peacefully in a Melbourne hospital on Monday, Nov. 23, local time, his family said. He was 83.
stories.summary: Ian “Molly” Meldrum, the broadcaster and music journalist who hosted the ABC’s Countdown and championed acts from INXS to Kylie Minogue, died peacefully in a Melbourne hospital on Monday, Nov. 23, local time, his family said. He was 83. On Countdown, which ran from 1974 to 1987, an endorsement from Meldrum (“do yourself a favour”) could make a record a hit, and his chaotic, Stetson-hatted interviews with stars became famous, including a nervous 1977 sit-down with the then Prince Charles. Earlier, while in London, he landed a scoop from John Lennon that the Beatles were splitting up, ABC News reported. In 2014 he became the first non-recording artist inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame. He had lived with a brain injury since a fall in 2011. King Charles called him “a true giant of the music industry”, Elton John also paid tribute, and Victoria’s premier said a state funeral will be held.
stories.why: Before streaming and algorithms, a single TV host could decide what a whole country listened to, and Meldrum was the clearest example. His push for local acts helped Australian musicians reach the world, a reminder of how much one passionate champion can matter to an industry.

stories.headline: COP31 climate talks collapse without a deal after the final text left out any mention of fossil fuels
stories.deck: The longest UN climate summit on record ended in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday, Nov. 22, with no main political agreement, the first such collapse since Copenhagen in 2009.
stories.summary: The longest UN climate summit on record ended in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday, Nov. 22, with no main political agreement, the first such collapse since Copenhagen in 2009. Talks were due to finish on Friday but ran into Sunday. A last-minute draft presented early Sunday did not contain the words “fossil fuels” at all; an earlier draft had mentioned them six times, which oil producers rejected, the BBC reported. The European Union, speaking through Irish minister Darragh O’Brien and EU climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra, refused to endorse a text that “does not even mention fossil fuels”, and Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu and others also objected. Poorer countries also complained that the text set no concrete figures for adaptation finance. Saudi Arabia’s delegate said Arab states had negotiated in good faith; Turkey’s COP31 president Murat Kurum said “there will be no new text”. UN Secretary-General António Guterres said he was “deeply disappointed”. Some side agreements survived: progress on a “just transition” mechanism, and more than 80 countries backed a target for electricity to meet 35% of global energy use by 2035. On Monday, Nov. 23, China’s foreign ministry called the outcome disappointing but said the green transition is “irreversible”.
stories.why: COPs work by consensus, so a handful of oil producers can block language the majority wants, and this time the majority refused to accept a weaker deal rather than paper over the split. The failure does not cancel the Paris Agreement or countries’ own plans, but it leaves no new global signal on fossil fuels or money for climate-hit countries just as the world is expected to pass 1.5C of warming. Expect pressure to reform how COPs make decisions.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement
stories.note: Updates the Nov 21 edition, which reported the talks running past their Friday deadline. The 35%-electrification goal (which China backed, Nov 21 edition) is a voluntary target, not part of a binding deal. China’s reaction comes from RTHK’s agency-based report of a foreign ministry briefing.

stories.headline: Democrats reach at least 258 House seats, their biggest majority since 1992, as Virginia Foxx concedes after a recount
stories.deck: Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx conceded North Carolina’s 5th District to Democrat Chuck Hubbard on Sunday, Nov. 22, after a recount left him 330 votes ahead.
stories.summary: Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx conceded North Carolina’s 5th District to Democrat Chuck Hubbard on Sunday, Nov. 22, after a recount left him 330 votes ahead. The machine recount netted Foxx one vote, NC Newsline reported. Foxx, 83, had held the seat since 2005; Hubbard, a former journalist, lost to her in 2024. With the result, Democrats have won at least 258 House seats to Republicans’ at least 173, with four races uncalled, the BBC reported, the most for either party since 1992. North Carolina’s delegation flips from 10 Republicans and four Democrats to 11 Democrats and three Republicans. “The peaceful transition of elected office from one person to another is one of the true hallmarks of our system of government,” Foxx said in her statement. Hubbard said he wanted to hold President Trump accountable and focus on the cost of living.
stories.why: A majority this large gives Democrats room to pass their own bills through the House and to run investigations of the administration from January without relying on every member. It also shows how far the cost-of-living backlash reached: districts like this one in north-western North Carolina were considered safely Republican.

stories.headline: Masked ICE officers arrest a father and daughter on a Seattle airport jet bridge, drawing outrage from the airport and Washington’s governor
stories.deck: Immigration officers detained two Mexican nationals as they boarded Alaska Airlines Flight 1306 to Los Angeles at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday morning, Nov. 21.
stories.summary: Immigration officers detained two Mexican nationals as they boarded Alaska Airlines Flight 1306 to Los Angeles at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday morning, Nov. 21. The Department of Homeland Security said Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza had overstayed his visa and that his daughter, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, “hurled hot coffee” at officers and would be charged with assaulting a federal officer. Their lawyer, Olia Catala, said they have no criminal record, that the father has a pending asylum claim and that the coffee was knocked from her hand when plain-clothes, masked officers lunged; an eyewitness told Reuters he did not see anyone throw coffee. The Port of Seattle, which runs the airport, said it was “outraged” and was asking whether agreed protocols were breached; Alaska Airlines said it had no advance notice, and the flight left more than two hours late with a new crew, CBS reported. Gov. Bob Ferguson called ICE “completely and totally out of control.” The two were being held at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, their lawyer said.
stories.why: Airports are where many immigrants with pending cases travel openly on their documents, so arrests at the gate spread fear well beyond this family. The clash between a federal agency and the local airport operator, and the dispute over the coffee, will matter in court: an assault charge can decide whether someone gets bond.

stories.headline: Army plans to detonate nearly five tonnes of unstable lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday despite a court pause, citing an emergency exemption
stories.deck: The Justice Department told a federal appeals court the Army will invoke an emergency exception to environmental rules to blow up degraded explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Middletown.
stories.summary: The Justice Department told a federal appeals court the Army will invoke an emergency exception to environmental rules to blow up degraded explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Middletown. The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals had paused the Environmental Protection Agency’s emergency permit after environmental groups sued, saying lead dust could travel far and safer options were not considered. Government lawyers argued that the roughly 9,700 pounds of lead azide in 68 barrels has formed unstable crystals and could “spontaneously explode” as temperatures drop below freezing, and that “a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion”. The filing said the Army would act by Tuesday, Nov. 24; on Sunday evening the Army said it now plans the detonation for Wednesday, Nov. 25, “to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced”. Earthjustice, representing the groups, argues the move would bypass the court.
stories.why: This is a test of how far the government can go around a court order by declaring an emergency. Residents face a real dilemma: an uncontrolled blast would be worse, but lead is toxic and families near the plant were given little notice. Watch whether the court responds before Wednesday.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement + Claim
stories.note: Planned, not confirmed: the detonation had not happened when sources were checked. Sources differ on when the government’s filing was made (late Saturday per the BBC and Al Jazeera; ABC says Sunday) and on whether the court’s pause came Thursday night or Friday. stories.deck: The two-time Cy Young winner’s contract would be the largest ever for a pitcher, according to people familiar with the deal; the Mets have not confirmed it pending a physical.

stories.headline: Big tech and police make final pitches as the Senate weighs Ottawa’s lawful-access bill, C-22
stories.deck: A Senate committee hears more witnesses on Monday, Nov. 23, and is scheduled to go through the bill clause by clause on Tuesday, CBC reports.
stories.summary: A Senate committee hears more witnesses on Monday, Nov. 23, and is scheduled to go through the bill clause by clause on Tuesday, CBC reports. Bill C-22 would give police and CSIS faster access to electronic data in investigations and could compel tech companies to adapt their systems to preserve and hand over information under warrant. After a backlash, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree amended it so providers would not have to decrypt data unless they supplied the encryption and hold the key, and cut metadata retention from one year to six months. But the bill still lets the minister issue confidential orders to companies. Signal has threatened to leave Canada if it passes as written, Meta said it would have to “consider” its options, and Google warned of secret surveillance directives. Police and child-protection groups urged senators to pass it quickly; one called the tech threats “a big bluff”. Any Senate amendments would send the bill back to the House of Commons.
stories.why: This is the kind of law that decides whether your messaging apps stay fully encrypted in Canada. The fight mirrors Britain’s clash with Apple, and senators now have to choose between police who say they are falling behind and companies and privacy advocates who say secret orders weaken everyone’s security.

stories.headline: More Canadian adults now use cannabis daily than drink alcohol daily, a CMAJ study of nearly 100,000 people finds

stories.summary: About 5.7% of adults reported daily or near-daily cannabis use in the 2023–24 Canadian Community Health Survey, compared with 5.2% for alcohol, with young adults driving the gap. The study, published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal, found daily cannabis use exceeded daily drinking in every age group from 18 to 49, and exceeded daily cigarette smoking among adults under 35, though cigarettes remained the most common daily habit overall at 8.5%. Among women aged 18 to 24, daily cannabis use (6.6%) was about 17 times the rate of daily drinking. Most daily users smoked cannabis rather than using edibles or other forms. “We have to take daily cannabis use pretty seriously,” lead author André McDonald of McMaster University told CBC.
stories.why: Canada was the first major country to fully legalise and market cannabis, so the world watches its data. For young adults the finding is the headline: daily cannabis is now more common than daily drinking among young adults, and most of it is smoked, which carries its own health risks.

stories.note: The survey is a one-time snapshot of self-reported use, not proof of a trend over time.

Together with uncontested, ex-officio and designated seats, the winners form the 1,500-member Election Committee, which will pick the chief executive next year and elect 40 of the 90 lawmakers in 2029. stories.deck: A preliminary-relief judge at the district court in The Hague found the Chinese carmaker’s seven-seat plug-in hybrid infringes Jaguar Land Rover’s EU design rights.

stories.headline: Zelensky says Ukrainian sea drones sank a Russian warship at a port in Libya; Russia has not commented
stories.deck: Ukraine’s president said seven naval drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury at Benghazi’s naval base on Sunday, Nov. 22, and also hit a Russian cargo ship off the Libyan coast.
stories.summary: Ukraine’s president said seven naval drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury at Benghazi’s naval base on Sunday, Nov. 22, and also hit a Russian cargo ship off the Libyan coast. In a statement on Monday, Nov. 23, Volodymyr Zelensky called it “an exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war”, saying a Ka-27 helicopter was also destroyed and that the cargo ship, the Angara, carried weapons. Authorities in eastern Libya said the warship had stopped to refuel on its way back to Russia. The BBC said satellite images from Vantor showed the corvette capsized with only its bow visible; Libya’s eastern health ministry said crew from the cargo ship had been rescued. The UN mission in Libya called for an independent investigation, and eastern Libyan commander Saddam Haftar rejected the use of Libyan territory “as an arena for settling scores”. Moscow had not commented, the BBC and Al Jazeera reported. Separately, Russian strikes on the Kyiv region killed at least 15 people overnight into Nov. 23, including 11 in a partly collapsed apartment block in Dymer, according to Ukrainian officials quoted by Al Jazeera.
stories.why: If confirmed, this would be one of Ukraine’s longest-range strikes yet, carried out in the Mediterranean, far from the Black Sea. It shows Kyiv is willing to hit Russian military assets wherever they operate, and it drags Libya, already split between rival governments, further into a war it has no part in. It came a day after a Russia-bound cargo ship was hit in the Gulf of Finland.
stories.label: Claim + Reported + Official statement
stories.note: The sinking and the weapons cargo are Zelensky’s claims; the BBC’s satellite and video checks support a ship being badly damaged and capsized at Benghazi. Russia’s side was not available. Casualty figures for the Kyiv-region strikes were still rising when sources were checked.

stories.headline: Kenya and DR Congo agree to restore full diplomatic ties after a three-year rift over eastern Congo’s rebels
stories.deck: Presidents William Ruto and Félix Tshisekedi agreed on Sunday, Nov. 22, to return ambassadors and restore full relations, at a summit in Oyo, Republic of the Congo.

Ties soured in 2023, when DR Congo accused Kenya of hosting the launch of a rebel alliance that includes M23, recalled its envoy and later refused to accredit Kenya’s ambassador. Tensions grew after Kenya named a consul-general to M23-held Goma and hosted Congolese opposition figures, including former President Joseph Kabila, in October 2025. According to statements from both leaders, they agreed to restore ambassador-level representation, revive a joint cooperation commission and respect each other’s sovereignty and non-interference, and to work together on trade, security and the Ebola outbreak. The BBC noted that more than 5,700 people have died of Ebola in DR Congo since May.
stories.why: Kenya is East Africa’s diplomatic and trade hub, and DR Congo’s war in the east has strained the whole region. Restoring ambassadors does not end the fighting, which the WHO says is disrupting the Ebola response, but it removes one quarrel that had blocked regional mediation.
