stories.headline: South Korea’s education minister resigns after chaotic anti-AI-cheating measures at the national college entrance exam
stories.deck: Choi Kyo-jin stepped down on Sunday, Nov. 22, taking responsibility for last-minute rules meant to stop AI-assisted cheating on the Suneung, sat by about 500,000 students.
stories.summary: Choi Kyo-jin stepped down on Sunday, Nov. 22, taking responsibility for last-minute rules meant to stop AI-assisted cheating on the Suneung, sat by about 500,000 students on Thursday, Nov. 19. The measures followed a confession by the top scorer in April’s national tax accountancy exam, who said he photographed questions with a micro-camera, sent them to an AI tool and checked answers on his phone. On exam day, the government sent three nationwide emergency alerts that made phones across the country sound at once, candidates had to cover shirt buttons that could hide cameras, and glasses were inspected; the ministry said 111 candidates were found with unauthorised smart devices. “I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance,” Choi said. President Lee Jae Myung accepted the resignation about an hour later and told Prime Minister Han Seong-sook to oversee follow-up measures, Yonhap reported.
stories.why: For millions of young Koreans the Suneung shapes university and career chances, so trust in it is a national issue. The episode shows how cheap AI tools plus tiny cameras are forcing exam systems everywhere to rethink security, and how heavy-handed fixes can punish honest students too.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement

stories.headline: NATO calls Russian missiles that came down in Poland a “grave violation”; Warsaw says it looks like a deliberate provocation
stories.deck: Two Russian missiles and a suspected jet-powered drone fell in south-eastern Poland during Russia’s huge overnight attack on Ukraine on Nov. 20, Polish officials said. No one was hurt.
stories.summary: Two Russian missiles and a suspected jet-powered drone fell in south-eastern Poland during Russia’s huge overnight attack on Ukraine on Nov. 20, Polish officials said. No one was hurt. Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said one object, a Kh-101 cruise missile, came down at Nowy Lipowiec about 50 km from the Ukrainian border; Al Jazeera reported the others fell at Rudnik nad Sanem and Molodycz. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it appeared to be “an intentional provocation”, timed to a two-week European military exercise in Poland preparing for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called it a “grave violation” of Polish airspace, and AP (via PBS) reported he was expected to visit Poland this weekend. On Nov. 21 Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski told the BBC the missiles had guidance systems, so it was “very unlikely” they had been knocked off course by Ukrainian electronic warfare. Russia had not commented, the BBC said. Separately, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told CNN that Vladimir Putin is “a killer”, after Donald Trump called the Russian leader his “friend” at the Shenzhen summit; Trump said on Nov. 20 that he “can’t speak” to whether Putin is a friend to the U.S.
stories.why: Russian weapons have strayed into NATO territory before, but this time they came down near an exercise for a postwar force in Ukraine, and Poland’s leaders are openly calling it deliberate. That makes it harder to shrug off just as U.S. envoys push peace talks. The real test is what NATO does next: Article 5, the collective-defence clause, is a political decision, and Poland also has the option of Article 4, which only triggers consultations.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement + Claim
stories.note: Accounts of distance differ: AP (via PBS) and Al Jazeera say one missile came down about 35 km from the exercise area; the BBC quotes Polish authorities as saying about 100 km. Both are given here. Russia’s intent is unconfirmed; “provocation” is the Polish government’s assessment.

stories.headline: AI sell-off sinks the S&P 500 3.7% into a correction; Nvidia falls about 14% and Anthropic gives back half its debut gain
stories.deck: The Nasdaq composite fell 5.3% on Friday, Nov. 20, and turned negative for 2026, as chip stocks led a broad retreat from AI-linked shares.
stories.summary: A sell-off in artificial-intelligence stocks pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7% on Friday, Nov. 20, putting it in a “correction” more than 10% below its Oct. 6 record, NPR reported, citing AP. The Nasdaq composite slid 5.3% and turned negative for the year; the Dow fell 1.9%. NPR said it was the S&P 500’s worst week since April 2025 and capped a seven-day losing streak. Chipmakers led the fall: AMD sank 13.3%, Micron 13.9% and Broadcom 12.1%. Nvidia closed down about 14% (13.7% to 13.8% depending on the outlet), its seventh straight weekly decline, the longest since 2008, CNBC reported, after a Reuters report, which the BBC said it had not confirmed, that the SEC is looking at its accounting. Anthropic, a day after its Nasdaq debut, fell 8.5% (BBC) to 9.1% (NPR), giving back about half its first-day gain but staying above its $83 IPO price. Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight.
stories.why: AI stocks drove most of Wall Street’s gains this year, so their slide now drags down the whole market, including the retirement and index funds many people hold. Analysts point to doubts about the huge spending on data centres, worries over Nvidia since Jensen Huang’s exit, and November’s midterm results, which strengthened candidates who favour tighter rules on data centres. One bad week isn’t a crash, but the market is now asking whether AI spending will pay off.

stories.headline: Anthropic mathematician says he used Claude to prove the Riemann hypothesis; experts say checking it will take a long time
stories.deck: Levent Alpöge says an unreleased version of Claude helped him produce a proof of maths’ most famous unsolved problem, more than 250,000 pages long. It has not been verified.
stories.summary: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician on Anthropic’s technical staff, said on Friday, Nov. 20, that over about six weeks he used a non-public version of the company’s Claude chatbot to produce a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the BBC and DW reported. The 1859 conjecture about how prime numbers are distributed is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s seven Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a $1 million prize. Alpöge wrote that the work generated more than 250,000 pages, written in the proof-checking language Lean, and that he had not yet mastered all the mathematics involved. He also acknowledged the announcement came a day after Anthropic’s stock-market debut, calling the timing “horrible” and rejecting a cynical reading. Mathematician Terence Tao said verification is still some way off. Clay Institute president Martin Bridson, quoted by AP via DW, called it “an announcement of historic significance” but said “the journey… to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult.”
stories.why: If the proof holds, it would be one of the biggest results in the history of mathematics and the strongest evidence yet that AI can do original research at the very top level. Until other mathematicians check it, though, it is a claim, and one that is unusually hard to check. Its timing, right after Anthropic’s IPO, means people will also scrutinise the motives behind it.
stories.label: Claim + Reported
stories.note: The proof is unverified. “Solved” in some headlines goes further than the sources: the BBC says the claim would be significant “if found to be correct”.

stories.headline: Jury convicts Los Angeles man of starting the fire that grew into the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire
stories.deck: Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, was found guilty of two federal charges at a retrial on Friday, Nov. 20, after his first trial ended with a deadlocked jury in June.
stories.summary: A federal jury in Los Angeles on Friday, Nov. 20, convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of starting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that smouldered in root systems and flared up again on Jan. 7 to become the Palisades Fire, one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. It killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800 buildings in Pacific Palisades and Malibu, the BBC reported. He was convicted on both counts, one for the original Lachman Fire and one for the Palisades Fire, AP (via PBS) reported. His first trial in June ended in a mistrial after jurors deadlocked 10-2 in favour of acquittal. At the retrial, prosecutors relied on phone location data, photos of his car near the trail, fire-camera images and witness testimony. His lawyers said they were disappointed but respected the verdict. Sentencing is scheduled for March 17; he faces five to 20 years on each charge.
stories.why: For families who lost homes and relatives, the verdict brings a measure of accountability nearly two years later. Many of them are still trying to rebuild, and arguments over how Los Angeles prepared for and handled the fires go on.

stories.headline: Grand Theft Auto VI took in $3.79 billion on its first day, Rockstar says, calling it the biggest entertainment launch ever
stories.deck: The figure is the publisher’s own estimate of worldwide retail sales through the end of launch day, Nov. 19.
stories.summary: Rockstar Games, part of New York-based Take-Two Interactive, said on Friday, Nov. 20, that Grand Theft Auto VI brought in $3.79 billion in day-one retail sales, based on company estimates through the end of Nov. 19, the day it launched. It called that a record for any entertainment product. The company also said the game sold 32.5 million units before release, a record across platforms, and has a Metacritic score of 99. According to AFP (via RTHK), that is nearly five times what Grand Theft Auto V took in during its first 24 hours in 2013. The game is out on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, after more than eight years in development and two delays.
stories.why: It shows how big video games now are as entertainment: by the company’s count, one game’s opening day beat any film or album launch. The number comes from Rockstar and hasn’t been independently audited, but it sets expectations for Take-Two’s next earnings and for the industry.

stories.headline: Martin Luther King Jr.’s handwritten draft of the “I Have a Dream” speech goes on public display for the first time
stories.deck: The seven-page draft, the only one known, is on show at Atlanta’s National Center for Civil and Human Rights through Sunday. It doesn’t include the words “I have a dream.”
stories.summary: The only known draft of Martin Luther King Jr.’s 1963 March on Washington speech, handwritten in blue ink on yellow legal paper, is on public display for the first time at the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta, NPR reported on Nov. 20. According to the centre’s CEO, Jill Savitt, King originally titled it “Normalcy Never Again”, and the draft doesn’t contain the famous “I have a dream” lines, which he improvised on the day. NPR said the document will be on exhibit through Sunday.

stories.headline: The Lancet retracts a 2006 Toronto study that blamed a baby’s death on codeine in breast milk, citing “falsification”
stories.deck: The case report by Motherisk founder Gideon Koren shaped breastfeeding and pain-relief guidance worldwide for two decades.
stories.summary: The Lancet has retracted a 2006 case report by Gideon Koren, founder of the Motherisk lab at Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids), which linked an Ontario baby’s 2005 death to codeine passed through his mother’s breast milk, CBC News reported on Nov. 21. The journal said omissions in the research amounted to “falsification”, after receiving the outcome of an investigation by SickKids’ research-integrity office. stories.headline: Hong Kong proposes fines of up to HK$10 million and five years’ jail for building works that cause death or injury, after the Wang Fuk Court fire
stories.deck: The plans would require permits for large-scale maintenance projects. Separately, the chief secretary said lawful memorials for the fire’s 168 victims are “absolutely permitted”.
stories.summary: Hong Kong’s Development Bureau has proposed tightening the Buildings Ordinance after last November’s Wang Fuk Court fire in Tai Po, RTHK reported on Nov. 20. Large-scale maintenance works, on buildings of four storeys or more with scaffolding covering a whole side across at least four floors, would no longer count as minor works: they would need a Buildings Department permit, prescribed plans and a supervision plan. Works that cause or may cause death, injury or property damage would become a new offence with maximum penalties of HK$10 million and five years in prison, up from HK$1 million and three years. Using substandard materials could bring HK$3 million and three years. Contractors found to have engaged in bribery or bid-rigging could be struck off registers for three years without a disciplinary hearing. The government aims to table the bill in January and bring it into force by mid-2027. Ahead of the Nov. 26 anniversary of the fire, which killed 168 people, Chief Secretary Eric Chan said lawful memorial events are “absolutely permitted”, while warning people to beware of those with “ulterior motives”.
stories.why: The fire showed how loosely big repair jobs were supervised in a city full of ageing high-rises. The proposed penalties are much stiffer, but they won’t take effect until mid-2027. The government’s comments on memorials, allowing them while warning about “hidden agendas”, show how politically sensitive the anniversary still is.

stories.headline: Research schooner Tara sails from Hong Kong on an 18-month mission to learn why Coral Triangle reefs are holding up
stories.deck: The crew of 16 plans 26 stopovers in six countries to test which corals best resist bleaching.
stories.summary: The French research schooner Tara has left Hong Kong after a stopover in early November for an 18-month expedition to the Coral Triangle, the waters around Indonesia, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, Timor-Leste and the Philippines, Hong Kong Free Press reported. The region holds about a third of the world’s coral reefs, and its coral cover has held steady while as much as half of the world’s reefs were lost over four decades, according to the report. The crew of 16 will make 26 stopovers covering about 50,000 km, picking up scientists from local partner institutions and exposing coral fragments to different temperatures to look for biomarkers of heat-resistant corals that could help restoration elsewhere. Tara, built in 1989 as the Antarctica, was designed to drift in polar ice.
stories.why: Most reef news is about corals dying. This expedition is trying to find out why some survive, which could tell conservationists which corals to replant as seas warm. That matters for Hong Kong’s own coral communities too.

stories.headline: China backs a voluntary goal to get 35% of energy from electricity by 2035 and says it will help others electrify
stories.deck: China and Australia signed a joint statement at COP31 endorsing the “35:35” target, as the summit itself stayed deadlocked.
stories.summary: China and Australia, which is leading the COP31 negotiations, signed a joint statement on Friday night, Nov. 20, welcoming efforts to raise electricity’s share of global final energy use to 35% by 2035 “on a voluntary basis”, the Guardian and DW reported. Wang Yi, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and senior adviser to the Chinese government, told the Guardian in an exclusive interview that “China will do our best to realise clean end-use electrification, and also help other countries to improve.” He said the 35% target was “no problem” for China but that requiring all of that electricity to be low-carbon would be “a little bit difficult, even for China.” According to the Guardian, the latest COP31 draft downgraded the electrification pledge to one of several voluntary options; DW said environmental groups warn the text does not specify renewable sources, so gas and coal power could count.
stories.why: China emits more than a quarter of the world’s greenhouse gases, so its support for faster electrification matters, and it is also the biggest maker of the batteries, panels and EVs that electrification depends on. The catch is in the details: a voluntary target that does not require clean power could let countries electrify on coal.

stories.headline: China-born Princeton PhD student detained by ICE after a science conference; judge bars her transfer out of Virginia
stories.deck: Eva Yi Xie, a neuroscience doctoral student who came to the U.S. as a minor and has a pending asylum claim, was detained at Reagan National Airport on Nov. 19.
stories.summary: Eva Yi Xie, a third-year Princeton neuroscience PhD student, was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement at Reagan National Airport on Thursday, Nov. 19, after presenting her research at the Society for Neuroscience conference in Washington, Gothamist and The Daily Princetonian reported. She was taken to an ICE holding facility in Chantilly, Va. Xie came to the U.S. from China in 2016 as a minor, attended the Bronx High School of Science and MIT, and has a pending asylum claim with an immigration court date in early 2028, her lawyer Kerry Doyle told the Princetonian. Her lawyers filed a habeas corpus petition arguing she was detained without a warrant. Late on Friday, Nov. 20, U.S. District Judge Anthony Trenga ordered ICE not to move her out of the Eastern District of Virginia and to respond by Wednesday. Princeton’s graduate school dean said the university had arranged legal counsel. ICE had not responded to requests for comment.
stories.why: The case is being watched by Chinese students and researchers in the U.S. and by universities worried about scholars travelling to conferences. The judge’s order keeps her case in Virginia for now; the question of whether her detention is lawful is still undecided.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: ICE had not commented in either report as checked; the reason for her detention has not been stated publicly.

stories.headline: How Chinese wuxia game Phantom Blade Zero became a hit after its studio dropped a punishing 66-lives rule
stories.deck: Beijing studio S-Game sold more than 4 million copies in 72 hours, after making the original death limit optional, Sixth Tone reports.
stories.summary: Phantom Blade Zero, a martial-arts action game from Beijing developer S-Game released on Oct. 29, sold more than 4 million copies in its first 72 hours and topped Steam’s bestseller chart, Sixth Tone reported on Nov. 19. Its creator originally planned a hard limit of 66 lives, mirroring the hero’s 66 days to find a new heart, but S-Game made that optional and added three difficulty settings. Founder Liang Qiwei called it “one of the countless difficult decisions” in development. The studio spent four years and a reported 300 million to 400 million yuan on the game, recruited Hong Kong action star Donnie Yen and brought martial-arts experts and traditional performers into motion capture. IGN gave it 9/10 and its PC version scored 88 on Metacritic, above Black Myth: Wukong’s 81. It is set in a fictional wuxia world Liang has been developing for about two decades.
stories.why: After Black Myth: Wukong, this is a second big Chinese action game to win over players worldwide, and with an original world rather than a familiar classic. The story of the dropped death limit is a common creative dilemma: an artistic vision versus what a wide audience will put up with.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: Single outlet. Sixth Tone is an English-language outlet owned by the state-backed Shanghai United Media Group. Sales and budget figures are as reported.

stories.headline: COP31 climate talks run past their deadline, deadlocked over whether the deal should mention fossil fuels
stories.deck: Negotiators in Antalya worked through the night into Saturday, Nov. 21, as a group led by France and Panama pushed to restore language on moving away from oil, gas and coal.
stories.summary: Negotiators at the COP31 UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, worked through the night into Saturday, Nov. 21, without agreeing a deal, the BBC reported. A late push led by France and Panama, backed by island states and several EU members including Spain, Belgium, Sweden and Finland, is trying to put a commitment to move away from fossil fuels back into the text after producers led by Saudi Arabia pressed for its removal. “It is not acceptable to have a COP… that does not even mention fossil fuels,” said Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro. Australia’s Chris Bowen, who is leading the negotiations, argued the summit is about implementation and clean energy. The African Group is pressing for more adaptation money. According to the BBC, the draft “Antalya Accords” would for the first time acknowledge that the 1.5C goal has been missed. A new and possibly final text was expected on Saturday; DW’s live page said the summit had been extended until consensus is reached.
stories.why: Two years after COP28 promised a “transition away” from fossil fuels, a final COP31 text with no mention of them would be a clear step back. Watch whether the France–Panama group holds out or settles for weaker language, and whether the text really does accept that the 1.5C limit has been passed.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement

stories.headline: UK and EU agree trade and youth mobility deals at their Brussels summit; Miliband says rejoining could be discussed in future
stories.deck: Prime Minister Andy Burnham and EU leaders announced agreements on food and drink standards, emissions trading and a youth scheme on Nov. 20, a decade after the Brexit vote.
stories.summary: The UK and the EU announced agreements on food and drink standards, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme at their Brussels summit on Friday, Nov. 20. Under the youth plan, 100,000 young Britons would be able to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with similar access for Europeans in the UK, the Guardian reported. Prime Minister Andy Burnham called it “a good day for Britain and Europe” and said the deal would add 0.5% to UK GDP; Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called it a “turning point”, DW reported. The Guardian said the deals could still be derailed within six months, because the EU has threatened to block them unless European students pay domestic-level fees at British universities. On Nov. 21 Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said “all options” would be on the table in future informal talks, including rejoining, while stressing the government is keeping its manifesto red lines in this parliament. Burnham said legislation would go to parliament next week.
stories.why: This is the biggest step back toward Europe since Brexit, and for young people the youth scheme is the headline. It is not finished yet: the tuition-fee dispute could still sink it, and the UK government’s 0.5% growth figure is its own estimate. Miliband’s remarks put rejoining back into mainstream debate, even if nothing changes before the next election.

stories.headline: Denmark says Russian intelligence was behind a foiled plot to kill a US-Ukrainian rapper, and expels Russia’s defence attaché
stories.deck: Danish intelligence says Russia “planned and initiated” an attempt to kill the rapper Kyivstoner at a concert near Copenhagen in September; Russia calls the claim unsubstantiated.
stories.summary: Denmark’s Security and Intelligence Service (PET) said on Nov. 20 that it assesses an assassination attempt on a Ukrainian-American citizen at a concert north of Copenhagen on Sept. 25 was “planned and initiated” by Russian intelligence services. Danish media named the target as the rapper Kyivstoner, real name Albert Vasiliev, the BBC reported. Police stopped three people in a car near the venue and found firearms and knives; PET says the would-be attackers were linked to the banned gang Loyal to Familia. Two people have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service; local media reported both pleaded not guilty. Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said Russia’s defence attaché must leave within seven days. Russia’s embassy called the allegations “unsubstantiated”, and Russian state media quoted Moscow as saying it would respond “accordingly”. On Nov. 21, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned what she called an attempt “orchestrated by Russian intelligence services”.
stories.why: European governments have warned for months that Russia is hiring local criminals for sabotage; this is one of the starkest accusations yet, and it involves an attack planned at a crowded public event. The two suspects have not been tried, and the Russian link is an intelligence assessment, not a court finding.
stories.label: Official statement + Allegation + Reported
stories.note: The Russian role is PET’s assessment and is denied by Russia; the criminal case against the two suspects has not been tried.

stories.dateLabel: Nov 20, 2026 (Crimean Bridge strikes covered Nov 17 and Nov 19)
stories.headline: Russia hits three Kyiv bridges in one of the war’s largest missile attacks, days after Ukraine’s Crimean Bridge strikes
stories.deck: Ballistic missiles hit three bridges over the Dnipro in Kyiv overnight into Friday, Nov. 20, and at least eight people were killed across Ukraine, officials said.
stories.summary: Russia struck Ukraine overnight into Friday, Nov. 20, with what Ukraine’s air force said were almost 100 missiles and about 400 drones, one of the largest attacks since the 2022 invasion, the BBC reported. Ballistic missiles hit three bridges over the Dnipro in Kyiv — the Podilskyi, Darnytskyi and Southern bridges — which were closed or restricted to traffic, and Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to avoid driving into the city. Casualty figures rose through the morning: CBC, citing Kyiv authorities, first reported three dead in the capital; Al Jazeera and the BBC, citing Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky, reported eight killed nationwide (six in Kyiv, according to Al Jazeera) and 28 injured. Strikes also hit railway stations, including one in Lviv where the mayor said two people died, and power generation, causing outages in Kyiv and other regions. Russia’s defence ministry said it targeted bridges used to move weapons. The attack came hours after Vladimir Putin vowed to respond to Ukraine’s strikes this week on the Crimean (Kerch) Bridge. Poland’s defence minister said Russian flying objects entered Polish airspace; the BBC quoted him saying a Russian cruise missile landed about 50 km inside Poland, while DW reported a flying object crashed in the Lublin region.
stories.why: The strikes show how quickly the war escalates around symbolic targets: Ukraine hit the bridge Putin built to Crimea, and Russia answered by cutting the bridges that hold Kyiv together. They also landed in the middle of new peace diplomacy — European leaders say they are ready for talks and U.S. envoy Jared Kushner says Moscow may accept NATO-style guarantees for Ukraine — which the Kremlin has pushed back on. Any Russian weapon landing in Poland, a NATO member, raises the stakes further.

stories.headline: Mayor Mamdani releases a plan to close Rikers Island’s jails by the end of 2032
stories.summary: New York City released its long-awaited plan on Friday, Nov. 20, to close the jails on Rikers Island by the end of 2032, Gothamist and NPR reported. Detainees would move to four new borough-based jails and three hospital units, and the island would be turned over to climate and sustainability projects. The plan depends on cutting the jail population to about two-thirds of today’s roughly 6,600 people, a target some advocates told Gothamist may be hard to meet. The city had already acknowledged it would miss the legally required August 2027 closure date. “It is long past time to close what’s been a moral stain on our city,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani told NPR. More than 50 people have died in city custody since 2022, nearly all held at Rikers, NPR reported.
stories.why: Rikers has been a byword for jail violence for decades, and closing it is one of Mamdani’s signature promises. The new borough jails are years behind schedule, so the real test is whether the city can shrink its jail population without new court fights or political backlash.

Pentagon chief information officer Kirsten Davies will take over in an acting capacity, according to CNBC and CBC; Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth congratulated her on X. Axios, cited by CNBC, reported that chief of staff Stephen Miller pushed for the change, and CBS and AFP sources said Cairncross was fired, the BBC reported. The White House had not publicly given a reason when this edition was prepared, but a White House official confirmed the departure to NBC and CBS, according to CNBC. The administration says there is no sign the outages were a coordinated attack.
stories.why: A permanent cyber director needs Senate confirmation, so the country’s top cyber-defence job is now held on an acting basis at a moment when outages are shaking public confidence. stories.headline: An interim U.S. trade deal would kick-start formal CUSMA review talks, LeBlanc says, but some tariffs will stay

Trump said they were “really making history” and called for talks on cutting nuclear arsenals; Putin said the three shared an interest in settling the war in Ukraine; Xi, who hosted, said peace among great powers keeps the world stable. Reports differ on how long the closed-door talks lasted: about 55 minutes (Al Jazeera), more than an hour (CBC) or an hour and 20 minutes (AFP via Hong Kong Free Press). No joint agreement had been reported when this edition was prepared, and NPR wrote that the leaders “offered few solutions toward peace.” Earlier in the day Trump met Putin, their first meeting since August 2025, and then Xi. Al Jazeera, citing Xinhua, reported Xi said nuclear weapons “should be comprehensively banned and thoroughly destroyed.” Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, on her first trip to China since her Taiwan remarks strained ties a year ago, said she wants a “constructive and stable relationship” with Beijing; Japanese media cited by AFP said she did not get a one-to-one meeting with Xi.
stories.why: The image of the three nuclear superpowers at one table was the main result so far, and that matters in itself: it signals that Washington is willing to deal with Beijing and Moscow together, which worries Kyiv, European capitals and smaller Asian countries that fear decisions being made over their heads. Watch for any follow-up on nuclear arms talks, which China has long refused to join, and for what each side later says was agreed on Ukraine and Iran.

stories.headline: Anthropic prices the biggest IPO on record, with Nasdaq trading due to start Thursday
stories.summary: AI company Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, said on Wednesday, Nov. 18, that it sold more than 956 million shares at $83 each, above its planned $70–$78 range, in the largest initial public offering on record. NPR reported the company raised about $79.4 billion, or more than $81.3 billion including shares sold by existing stockholders; counting a further $26 billion in private share sales to companies including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, NPR put the total haul at more than $107 billion. The price values the five-year-old company at about $1.5 trillion (CBC: $1.51 trillion, including unvested employee options). Its shares were scheduled to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday, Nov. 19, under the ticker ANT; trading had not started when this edition was prepared. Previous record: SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June.
stories.why: The listing is the first big public test of how much investors will pay for a pure AI company after weeks of worry about an AI bubble; the Nasdaq is down more than 11% since early October, NPR said. How the shares trade will shape OpenAI’s own plans to list and the cost of money for the wider AI build-out.

stories.headline: Van Gogh’s “Chestnut Trees in Blossom” sells for a record $190.4 million in New York after a Nazi-era dispute is settled
stories.summary: Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (Chestnut Trees in Blossom), painted in Auvers-sur-Oise in 1890 in the last months of his life, sold at Sotheby’s in New York on Wednesday, Nov. 18, for $190.4 million, a record for the artist at auction; the previous high was $117.2 million in 2022. Hours before the sale, Sotheby’s said it had resolved a dispute between the sellers, the Blaquier-Arrieta family, and heirs of German publisher Samuel Fischer, whose family sold the painting in 1936 and who argued it was given up because of losses suffered under the Nazis. The Guardian, citing The New York Times, reported the buyer was dealer William Acquavella; the BBC said the buyer was not immediately clear.
stories.why: The sale shows the top of the art market is still strong despite wider economic worries, and that restitution claims over Nazi-era sales now shape how and when major works can be sold. The terms of the settlement were not disclosed.

stories.headline: Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo hippo who survived a premature birth, is under round-the-clock care after swallowing a hat
stories.summary: The Cincinnati Zoo says Fiona, the hippo who became famous after surviving a premature birth in 2017, is receiving emergency medical care after swallowing a knit hat that ended up in her enclosure about nine days earlier, BBC reported on Wednesday, Nov. 18. A zoo spokesperson said a visitor tossed the hat in the air, it caught on a ceiling fan and was flung through a small opening. Fiona showed no symptoms at first but then lost her appetite; staff are giving fluids and ultrasounds, and the latest scan showed the hat moving through her small intestine, though she remains a bit dehydrated. CBC said she is on 24-hour medical watch.
stories.why: Fiona’s fight to survive as a tiny premature calf made her one of the best-known zoo animals in the world, so her health draws wide attention. The case is also a reminder of why zoos ask visitors not to throw anything near animals.

stories.why: Canada’s auto and steel towns are paying for the tariff fight in lost jobs and closed plants. Carney’s message is that Canada will keep building other markets, including China, if talks stall, a strategy that adds leverage but also risks angering Washington further.

stories.headline: Gas prices are falling across Canada as more oil moves through the Strait of Hormuz
stories.summary: The national average price of gas was $1.514 a litre on Wednesday, Nov. 18, about eight cents lower than a week earlier and 29.4 cents below the average 30 days ago, according to price tracker affordableenergy.ca, CBC reported. GasBuddy analyst Patrick De Haan said prices in Manitoba and Saskatchewan were down by more than 30 cents from last month and some Calgary stations were below $1 a litre, and could fall another five to 10 cents in coming weeks if there are no new shocks in the U.S. war with Iran. Analysts credited more tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, helped by U.S. military escorts, and seasonal factors; Brent crude is just under US$92 a barrel, down from about US$116 in mid-October. Prices remain higher than a year ago.
stories.why: Fuel is one of the fastest ways the Iran war reaches household budgets, so falling pump prices give some relief heading into winter. The relief depends on shipping through Hormuz staying open, which is outside Canada’s control.

stories.headline: High school students across New Brunswick walk out over a coming full cellphone ban
stories.summary: Hundreds of high school students in New Brunswick walked out of class on Wednesday afternoon, Nov. 18, to protest a broader ban on personal phones in schools, CBC reported. Walkouts were planned at 73 schools; CBC confirmed large turnouts in Saint John, Moncton (more than 200 students at Moncton High) and Fredericton’s Leo Hayes High, but had not verified participation elsewhere. Phones have been banned in all classrooms since September; high school students can still use them at lunch and between classes, but will fall under a total ban when the second semester starts early in 2027. Students said they were not consulted. Education Minister Claire Johnson was not made available for an interview.
stories.why: School phone bans are spreading across Canada and the U.S., usually with strong support from parents and teachers. Organised student pushback like this is rarer, and how the province responds may shape whether students get a say in similar rules elsewhere.

stories.headline: Hong Kong’s Election Committee subsector elections are set for Sunday, with 856 candidates for 723 seats
stories.summary: The 2026 Election Committee Subsector Ordinary Elections are scheduled for Sunday, Nov. 22, from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., the Registration and Electoral Office said on Thursday, Nov. 19. stories.summary: The International Court of Justice in The Hague ruled on Thursday, Nov. 19, in the case brought by The Gambia, finding that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians in the 2017 military crackdown and acted with “genocidal intent” in specific cases, Al Jazeera reported. Court President Yuji Iwasawa said evidence showed some 10,000 Rohingya were killed; the court also said Myanmar violated its obligation to prevent genocide. Myanmar has said the operations were a response to attacks by Rohingya fighters. More than 730,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh, and about 1.2 million live in camps in Cox’s Bazar. stories.headline: Xi tells APEC business leaders to defend free trade, then says China and Russia should “lead” a multipolar world
stories.deck: In a keynote to the APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday, Xi Jinping called for upholding the WTO-centred trading system and pledged to lower tariffs and widen market access. After talks with Vladimir Putin, he said Beijing and Moscow should lead the move towards a multipolar world, Al Jazeera reported.
stories.summary: In a keynote to the APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday, Xi Jinping called for upholding the WTO-centred trading system and pledged to lower tariffs and widen market access. After talks with Vladimir Putin, he said Beijing and Moscow should lead the move towards a multipolar world, Al Jazeera reported. “Stability brings security; security brings prosperity,” Xi said, according to RTHK, and he called for progress towards a Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific. Al Jazeera read his warnings about “unilateralism and protectionism” as veiled criticism of Donald Trump’s tariffs. In their meeting, Xi said China–Russia relations had stayed “as solid as a mountain,” and Putin said two-way trade had passed US$200 billion, RTHK reported; it was their fifth meeting this year. Speaking to the summit afterwards, Putin called Western powers “former hegemons” and said Europe was in a “humiliating decline,” according to Al Jazeera. Hong Kong leader John Lee said on Facebook that Xi’s speech had encouraged him and that Hong Kong could be a springboard for businesses entering the Greater Bay Area.
stories.why: Xi is presenting China as the steady defender of open trade on the eve of meeting Trump, while standing visibly beside Putin. That framing will shape how Asian governments and companies read Thursday’s three-way meeting, and whether they see Beijing or Washington as the more predictable partner.

stories.headline: Ukrainian strike brings down part of the Kerch bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, images show
stories.deck: A large arched section of the road bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea appears to have collapsed into the Kerch Strait after an overnight Ukrainian attack, the BBC and the Guardian report. Volodymyr Zelensky called it an “unprecedented” operation; the Kremlin says the bridge will be rebuilt.
stories.summary: A large arched section of the road bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea appears to have collapsed into the Kerch Strait after an overnight Ukrainian attack, the BBC and the Guardian report. Volodymyr Zelensky called it an “unprecedented” operation; the Kremlin says the bridge will be rebuilt. Zelensky said the strike capped a seven-stage operation in which Ukrainian forces first knocked out air defences, radars and electronic-warfare equipment, then hit the road section with drones and the parallel rail line with missiles. The Guardian said photos suggested a 227-metre road arch had fallen and the adjacent railway arch was damaged; the BBC said the rail arch was still standing and a Russian-backed official said some rail services were running. Crimea’s Russian-installed governor, Sergei Aksyonov, said traffic had been suspended. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would be restored and “even better than before,” and Russia’s Investigative Committee opened a terrorism case. Early on Tuesday the Associated Press, quoted by NPR, said it could not yet verify reports of a collapse. Russia’s Defence Ministry reported its largest Ukrainian drone attack of the war for a second straight night — 1,441 drones downed, according to NPR’s AP report, and 2,256 according to the BBC. Overnight, Russian strikes hit Kyiv’s Northern and Southern bridges over the Dnipro and disrupted heating and water; NPR reported at least two people killed.
stories.why: The bridge, opened by Vladimir Putin in 2018, is Russia’s only direct road and rail link to Crimea and a symbol of the 2014 annexation. If the span is down for long, supplies must move by ferry or along a land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine that Ukrainian drones already target, and debris may block shipping to Sea of Azov ports. Coming two days before Putin is due to meet Xi Jinping and Donald Trump in Shenzhen, the strike also undercuts his image of strength.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement + Claim

stories.headline: Freeman Johnson, the oldest remaining Pearl Harbor survivor, dies at 106
stories.deck: Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the few remaining survivors of the Dec. 7, 1941, attack on Pearl Harbor, died on Saturday at his home in Centerville, Massachusetts, his daughter told the Associated Press. He was 106.
stories.summary: Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the few remaining survivors of the Dec. 7, 1941, attack on Pearl Harbor, died on Saturday at his home in Centerville, Massachusetts, his daughter told the Associated Press. He was 106. Johnson was working below deck on a boiler of the light cruiser USS St. Louis during the Japanese attack and told the AP in May that he neither saw nor heard it — “I was inside a steam drum.” He later helped commission the battleship USS Iowa and watched Japan’s surrender in Tokyo Bay from the Iowa’s mast in September 1945. After the war he worked in a machinist shop, a convenience store and delivering meals to seniors, retiring from that last job at 90. The list of known survivors had stood at about a dozen names after the death of Ira “Ike” Schab, 105, in December 2025.
stories.why: With the 85th anniversary of Pearl Harbor three weeks away, only a handful of people who were there are still alive. Johnson’s matter-of-fact memories — of missing the attack entirely below deck — are a reminder of how ordinary most of the sailors were.

stories.deck: Meeting in Shenzhen on Tuesday ahead of APEC, Mark Carney and Xi Jinping agreed that China will drop a 25 per cent tariff on frozen pork cuts and several seafood products, worth about $400 million in Canadian exports a year, Carney’s office said.
stories.summary: Meeting in Shenzhen on Tuesday ahead of APEC, Mark Carney and Xi Jinping agreed that China will drop a 25 per cent tariff on frozen pork cuts and several seafood products, worth about $400 million in Canadian exports a year, Carney’s office said. The list includes frozen cold-water shrimp, Greenland halibut, some mollusks and sea cucumber, Global News reported. In return, Canada will extend tariff relief to 32 more Chinese steel and aluminum items for which Canadian supply is short, and its existing remission measures will run two more years. China also agreed to open its market to Canadian fava beans, chickpeas and lentils; the two sides plan a major Canadian trade mission in 2027 and have named next year a “year of e-commerce.” Carney hailed “greater predictability and stability” and said Canada was ahead of schedule on its goal of raising exports to China “by 50% by the end of this decade,” DW reported. Xi, according to Xinhua as carried by RTHK, set out four proposals for relations and said exchanges had fully resumed. Before the trip, Carney said he would raise foreign interference, which Beijing denies. On Monday, U.S. trade adviser Peter Navarro called Carney’s suggestion that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if talks with Washington fail “offensive in the extreme.”
stories.why: Ottawa is using China to cut its dependence on the U.S. market while trade talks with Washington drag on. That brings quick wins for farmers and fishers, but it also feeds the White House’s anger and Canadian worries about security and election interference.

stories.headline: Quebecor makes a $31-billion bid for Telus, whose board says the offer carries significant risks
stories.deck: Quebecor, owner of Videotron, Freedom Mobile and Fizz, has proposed to buy Telus in a cash-and-shares deal it values at about $31 billion, a premium of roughly 60 per cent. Telus’s board says it is reviewing the offer but has serious concerns.
stories.summary: Quebecor, owner of Videotron, Freedom Mobile and Fizz, has proposed to buy Telus in a cash-and-shares deal it values at about $31 billion, a premium of roughly 60 per cent. Telus’s board says it is reviewing the offer but has serious concerns. Under the non-binding proposal, Telus shareholders would get $6.35 in cash and 0.17 of a Quebecor share for each Telus share. Quebecor said it first approached Telus in June and sent an enhanced offer this month; it says it would keep the Telus brands and that a combined company could invest more in 5G and rural connectivity. Telus board chair John Manley said Quebecor had yet to explain how the deal could win approval under Canada’s telecom rules and disputed its valuation, and that Telus would keep engaging with Quebecor, the government and regulators while exploring alternatives. Any deal would need approval from the Competition Bureau, the CRTC and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada; Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said it would be reviewed “independently and rigorously.”
stories.why: Quebecor became Canada’s low-price challenger by buying Freedom Mobile; taking over Telus would turn it into one of the giants and cut the number of national carriers. Experts cited by CBC say the deal would make the market less competitive and could affect phone bills, so regulators’ verdict matters to customers, not just shareholders.

stories.summary: Nicholas Herring of Murray Harbour, P.E.I., won the 2026 Giller Prize on Monday night in Toronto for Your Breath in Charcoal, his second novel. For the first time, the winner was chosen by a jury of independent booksellers. The novel follows Knickle, an East Coast “everyman” on a road trip from P.E.I. to Toronto; CBC describes it as the story of two Islanders in the late 1990s trying to make it in Ontario’s construction industry. stories.why: The Giller is Canada’s richest fiction prize and reliably lifts sales, so a small Atlantic press and a writer who still fishes for a living are about to get national attention. stories.headline: Meta tells senators it would have to consider pulling encrypted services from Canada if the lawful-access bill passes unchanged
stories.deck: Meta representatives told a Senate committee on Monday evening that Bill C-22 could leave the company unable to offer secure end-to-end encryption in Canada, and that it would have to “consider” withdrawing such services if the bill passes as is.
stories.summary: Meta representatives told a Senate committee on Monday evening that Bill C-22 could leave the company unable to offer secure end-to-end encryption in Canada, and that it would have to “consider” withdrawing such services if the bill passes as is. The lawful-access bill would require tech companies to be able to hand over information to investigators with a warrant and would let the public safety minister issue confidential orders requiring them to build in surveillance capabilities, subject to review by the intelligence commissioner. Meta’s privacy policy director, Robyn Greene, said the law would be impossible to comply with “and still offer secure, end-to-end encrypted services.” Signal told the committee it would leave Canada rather than compromise users’ security, and Apple has said the government’s amendments are not enough. The government argues police need the tools to fight modern crime; it has already narrowed when companies must decrypt data and cut metadata retention to six months.
stories.why: WhatsApp, Signal and iMessage are how millions of Canadians talk, so a standoff over encryption could change everyday communication. The Senate committee’s next moves will show whether Ottawa adds stronger protections or tests the companies’ threats.

stories.deck: Shanghai authorities have dismissed two researchers after investigators found ignored safety warnings, weak ethics review and undisclosed money and gifts from the family in a gene-editing trial that ended in a child’s death, Sixth Tone reported.
stories.summary: Shanghai authorities have dismissed two researchers after investigators found ignored safety warnings, weak ethics review and undisclosed money and gifts from the family in a gene-editing trial that ended in a child’s death, Sixth Tone reported. The family had contributed 5.3 million yuan (about US$800,000) to the research and separately gave researchers about 1.06 million yuan in money and gifts, investigators said. Qiu Zilong and Yang Kan were dismissed and barred from science programmes for five years; hospital officials were demoted, and the city plans special inspections of clinical research on new biomedical technologies.
stories.why: China is racing to lead in gene and cell therapies, and this case shows how experimental treatment can outrun safeguards. Stricter oversight of such trials is likely to follow.

stories.headline: China adds a CAR T-cell cancer therapy to its national health insurance for the first time, from Jan. 1

stories.deck: Denmark, the Netherlands, Germany, Austria and Greece announced on Monday that they are working with Rwanda on a “return hub” for migrants who have no legal right to stay in the European Union. A formal agreement has not yet been signed.
stories.summary: Denmark, the Netherlands, Germany, Austria and Greece announced on Monday that they are working with Rwanda on a “return hub” for migrants who have no legal right to stay in the European Union. A formal agreement has not yet been signed. Unlike Britain’s abandoned Rwanda plan, which would have sent people there while their claims were processed, the scheme would cover only people whose asylum applications have already been rejected and who cannot be returned home. They could settle in Rwanda, go home or move to another country that admits them. The governments, which would pay the costs, did not say how many people would be sent. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the plan would “break down the business model of human smugglers.” Rwanda’s interior minister said Kigali was not planning for thousands to stay. Human Rights Watch called the plan “utterly deplorable,” and 47 organisations urged the countries to scrap it.
stories.why: The five governments call it a pilot and a deterrent, so if it goes ahead other European states may copy it. Critics point out that Europe has repeatedly raised concerns about Rwanda’s human rights record and its support for the M23 armed group in eastern Congo.

The 18-page draft, released on Monday in Antalya, Türkiye, also includes co-host Türkiye’s goal of raising electrification of the world economy to 35 per cent by 2035, expresses “deep concern” that the 1.5C warming limit is now out of reach, and calls for rapidly scaling up carbon capture and removal. stories.headline: ULA’s Vulcan rocket fails 10 minutes after launch, destroying 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites
stories.deck: A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed about 10 minutes after lifting off from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on Sunday, losing all 40 satellites it was carrying for Amazon’s Leo broadband network in the company’s first outright mission failure.
stories.summary: A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed about 10 minutes after lifting off from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on Sunday, losing all 40 satellites it was carrying for Amazon’s Leo broadband network in the company’s first outright mission failure. ULA, a Boeing–Lockheed Martin joint venture formed in 2006, said the vehicle “suffered an anomaly” and that it did not yet have data on the cause. Ars Technica, citing unnamed sources, reported that the problem occurred in the booster stage rather than the upper stage or strap-on boosters. It was Vulcan’s fifth flight and its first in about nine months, after separate investigations into its solid rocket boosters and its BE-4 main engines, and the first of 38 Vulcan launches Amazon has booked for its planned constellation of more than 3,200 satellites. The failure is expected to ground the rocket, which also carries about half of the U.S. military’s national-security launches in the coming years, Ars reported.
stories.why: Amazon is racing SpaceX’s Starlink, and its main launch provider is now grounded for an unknown period. With the Pentagon also relying on Vulcan, the loss deepens U.S. dependence on SpaceX at a time when competition in launch was supposed to be growing.

stories.headline: NTSB says the tanker that hit a docked New Orleans riverboat had a steering failure that left its rudder stuck
stories.deck: Federal investigators said on Sunday that the tanker Atlantic Asphalt suffered a “steering casualty” that kept its rudder turned to starboard before it struck the docked riverboat American Heritage on the Mississippi on Friday.
stories.summary: Federal investigators said on Sunday that the tanker Atlantic Asphalt suffered a “steering casualty” that kept its rudder turned to starboard before it struck the docked riverboat American Heritage on the Mississippi on Friday. The exact cause of the steering problem has not been determined, investigator-in-charge Bart Barnum said, adding that the voyage data recorder captured a warning signal and orders to drop anchor and take emergency action minutes before the crash. The American Heritage, carrying 140 passengers and 50 crew, capsized within 22 minutes, ABC News reported, citing the NTSB; more than 30 people were injured and all aboard were accounted for. A preliminary NTSB report is expected in about 30 days. The Port of New Orleans has separately sued the tanker’s owners.

stories.headline: Voyager 1 is set to become the first spacecraft one light-day from Earth on Wednesday, and NASA wants the world to flash it a message
stories.deck: NASA says Voyager 1, launched in 1977, will reach a distance of one light-day from Earth — about 16 billion miles — at 5:16:07 a.m. EST on Wednesday, Nov. 18, and is inviting people to flash its call sign at the sky on Tuesday night.
stories.summary: NASA says Voyager 1, launched in 1977, will reach a distance of one light-day from Earth — about 16 billion miles — at 5:16:07 a.m. EST on Wednesday, Nov. 18, and is inviting people to flash its call sign at the sky on Tuesday night. A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, so a command sent to the probe will take a day to arrive and another day for a reply to return. For “Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day,” NASA is asking people to blink “VGR” in Morse code with phones or flashlights after sunset on Nov. 17. Voyager 1 flew past Jupiter and Saturn, became the most distant human-made object in 1998 and entered interstellar space in 2012. NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory plans a public discussion with mission members on Nov. 19.
stories.why: A nearly 50-year-old spacecraft still sending data from interstellar space is one of engineering’s great endurance stories, and the milestone is an easy invitation for anyone to take part — no telescope required.

stories.deck: Quarterback Cody Fajardo threw two touchdown passes and ran for two more as the Edmonton Elks beat the Montreal Alouettes 37-30 in Calgary on Sunday for their first Grey Cup since 2015.

Vincent Blanchard’s late field goals sealed it after Montreal turned the ball over on downs with 1:40 left. The Elks finished last in the West Division a season ago; it is their 15th championship. Maciej Hatta said.

stories.deck: Nolan Aziz, Will Vyse and Georges Kirijian, all 24 and from Toronto, paddled ashore at Jericho Beach on Sunday after 219 days and about 8,000 kilometres from Tadoussac, Quebec, raising money for remote northern Indigenous communities.

stories.summary: Shares of New World Development fell more than 45% at Monday’s open to HK$2.655, an all-time low since its 1980 listing, after the heavily indebted developer proposed raising about HK$24.9 billion through a deeply discounted rights issue. The plan offers 11 new shares for every share held at HK$0.90 each, 81.5% below Friday’s close of HK$4.87, according to a company filing reported by RTHK. About a third of the proceeds would prepay 10% of roughly HK$82 billion in bank loans, with the rest of those loans extended by two years, and another third would repay other debt. Controlling shareholder Chow Tai Fook Enterprises, which owns about 45.3%, has committed to take up its full entitlement, and the rest is underwritten. JP Morgan said the discount was likely beyond most investors’ expectations and that the money would ease, but not end, the company’s liquidity stress.
stories.why: New World is one of Hong Kong’s best-known developers, and asking shareholders for more than three times its remaining market value shows how deep the property slump has cut. Its fate is a bellwether for lenders and other developers in the city.

stories.headline: China confirms Xi will host the first-ever summit with Trump and Putin in Shenzhen on Thursday
stories.deck: China’s foreign ministry said on Monday that Xi Jinping will hold a China‑Russia‑US heads‑of‑state meeting with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen on Nov. 19, the first face‑to‑face meeting of the three countries’ leaders. Trump is due in Manila for the ASEAN summit first.
stories.summary: China’s foreign ministry said on Monday that Xi Jinping will hold a China‑Russia‑US heads‑of‑state meeting with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen on Nov. 19, the first face‑to‑face meeting of the three countries’ leaders. Trump is due in Manila for the ASEAN summit first. Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said the leaders would “exchange in-depth views on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability,” calling the meeting of “groundbreaking significance,” RTHK reported. The White House and the Kremlin had already confirmed the three-way meeting, which is planned on the sidelines of the APEC leaders’ gathering in the city. Trump wants to discuss reducing nuclear arsenals and the Iran war, but U.S. officials said Russia’s war in Ukraine is not expected to be on his agenda, according to AFP via Hong Kong Free Press. A White House official told NPR that no agreement on denuclearization is expected and called the meeting an “entry point”; China has long said the U.S. and Russia should cut their own arsenals before it joins such talks. Trump stops first in Manila for the ASEAN summit, where the Guardian says he is expected to sign a trade agreement with Thailand; NPR reports that Elon Musk is joining him in Shenzhen. It is Trump’s first overseas trip since his party’s heavy losses in this month’s midterm elections.
stories.why: A three-way meeting of the U.S., Chinese and Russian leaders has never happened before, and the setting lets Xi play host to both. Expectations of concrete deals are low, so the signals that come out — on nuclear arms, Iran, trade and whether Ukraine is raised at all — will matter more than any communiqué.
stories.label: Official statement + Reported

stories.headline: Fire at a motorcycle rental shop in Phuket’s Patong kills 11 people, mostly from smoke
stories.deck: A pre-dawn fire that started at a motorcycle rental business in Patong, on Thailand’s resort island of Phuket, killed 11 people on Monday and spread through neighbouring shophouses, police said.
stories.summary: A pre-dawn fire that started at a motorcycle rental business in Patong, on Thailand’s resort island of Phuket, killed 11 people on Monday and spread through neighbouring shophouses, police said. The blaze was reported at about 3:17 a.m. local time; officials said about 100 motorcycles, fuel, oil, tyres and plastics fed thick, toxic smoke that trapped people living on the upper floors, and most of the dead are believed to have died from smoke inhalation. Police said an initial investigation pointed to an exploding electrical transformer or a short circuit on a utility pole, and ruled out arson. Injury counts differ: Al Jazeera, citing police, reported 16; the Phuket News, citing a later police update, 18; the Nation reported 36 taken to hospital. Authorities said no tourists were among the dead or injured, according to Al Jazeera.
stories.why: Patong is one of Asia’s busiest tourist strips, and the deaths of workers living above a shop full of fuel and motorcycles point to a familiar problem: mixed-use buildings with weak fire separation. Expect pressure on Thai authorities over inspections, months after another deadly fire.

The French Open champion did not drop a set all week and lost only 26 games in five matches, the BBC reported. She rises to No. 2 in the world, 293 points behind Elena Rybakina going into 2027. The players did not shake hands after the match, Al Jazeera noted; Ukrainian players have declined to shake hands with Russian and Belarusian opponents since Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion, in line with their federation’s policy. Andreeva also won a custom purple Mercedes — though, at 19, she said she still needs a driver’s licence.
stories.why: Andreeva’s dominance makes her a clear challenger for No. 1 next season. The final was also another reminder of how the war in Ukraine still shapes the women’s tour.

stories.headline: SpaceX catches a Starship spacecraft returning from orbit for the first time, after losing the booster
stories.deck: SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship rocket with the launch tower’s mechanical arms in Starbase, Texas, on Saturday, about 22 hours after liftoff. The Super Heavy booster, which SpaceX had also hoped to catch, aborted and exploded over the Gulf of Mexico on Friday.
stories.summary: SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship rocket with the launch tower’s mechanical arms in Starbase, Texas, on Saturday, about 22 hours after liftoff. The Super Heavy booster, which SpaceX had also hoped to catch, aborted and exploded over the Gulf of Mexico on Friday. The 124-metre (407-foot) rocket lifted off from Starbase on Friday afternoon on its 15th full-scale test flight, the first in which SpaceX tried to recover both stages. Minutes after launch the booster triggered an automated abort and diverted to the ocean, where it exploded; Elon Musk said it had been “slightly low on fuel,” the BBC reported. The ship went on to deploy 26 Starlink satellites, circled Earth 14 times and then flew back to the tower, where the “chopsticks” arms caught it. SpaceX said the spacecraft, including its heat shield, appeared to work well, according to NPR. NASA, which is paying SpaceX to use Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon, welcomed the result. SpaceX had already caught boosters three times on earlier flights.
stories.why: A rocket whose two stages can both be flown again is what would make Starship cheap enough for moon landings, huge satellite launches and Musk’s Mars plans. Catching the spacecraft is the harder half of that goal, but the lost booster shows the full system still isn’t routine.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: Duffy ties the nationwide ground stop to contractor work replacing copper wiring, but the FAA says the root cause is still unknown
stories.deck: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday’s nationwide ground stop followed upgrade work by contractor L3Harris to switch air traffic control communications from copper wire to fibre, after a router flooded other equipment with connection attempts. The FAA said flight schedules should be back to normal by the end of Sunday.
stories.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday’s nationwide ground stop followed upgrade work by contractor L3Harris to switch air traffic control communications from copper wire to fibre, after a router flooded other equipment with connection attempts. The FAA said flight schedules should be back to normal by the end of Sunday. At a Saturday news conference, Duffy said a router at “at least” one remote site sent more than 1,000 connection attempts roughly every five seconds, disrupting radio and radar feeds, CNBC reported. He said investigators were trying to determine whether the cause was “incompetence” — an installation error — or a faulty router. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said there was “zero evidence” of anything nefarious, that no FAA facility went dark, and that the agency grounded flights because it could not explain the instability; CNBC reported that the root cause had not been pinned down. L3Harris said it is supporting the FAA investigation and has completed more than 70% of the copper-to-fibre conversion. The BBC, citing flight-tracking data, said more than 15,000 U.S. flights were delayed or cancelled on Friday and more than 5,900 cancelled and 7,000 delayed on Saturday.
stories.why: Officials had first blamed old equipment; now the spotlight is on the work meant to replace it. Who is found responsible — the contractor, the hardware or the FAA’s own oversight — will shape the fight in Congress over the billions Duffy wants to modernize air traffic control.
stories.label: Reported + official statement
stories.note: Ongoing story first reported in the Nov 14 edition. The cause is the administration’s account so far; the FAA said the root cause had not been established. Flight counts are flight-tracking tallies cited by the BBC.

stories.headline: Judge temporarily blocks Trump’s plan to close a historic Washington public golf course for a 15-month rebuild
stories.deck: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued a temporary restraining order on Saturday, a day before East Potomac Golf Links was due to close for President Trump’s planned redevelopment into a championship-level course.
stories.summary: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued a temporary restraining order on Saturday, a day before East Potomac Golf Links was due to close for President Trump’s planned redevelopment into a championship-level course. NPR said the order delays any work at the site for two weeks. The challenge was brought in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers, who argue the plan would change the character of the public course and make it unaffordable; Trump denies that. In her 30-page ruling, the BBC reported, Reyes wrote that the government’s justifications were pretextual, that it had violated at least two federal laws “to meet an arbitrary deadline,” and that closing a park “daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes” ran against the public interest. She also said the administration could not close the park or course but was not required to actively manage them. Trump had announced on Oct. 26 that the course would close on Nov. 15. The BBC said it had asked the White House for comment.
stories.why: The ruling tests how far a president can remake federal parkland around the capital on his own timetable. For now, a 106-year-old public course stays open while the case proceeds.

stories.headline: Port of New Orleans sues the tanker’s owners over the cruise-boat collision, and a judge lets federal officials take control of the ship
stories.deck: The port says the tanker Atlantic Asphalt caused at least $1 million in damage when it struck the docked river cruise boat American Heritage on Friday, and alleges negligence by its owner and managers. A judge issued a warrant giving federal officials control of the ship for now.
stories.summary: The port says the tanker Atlantic Asphalt caused at least $1 million in damage when it struck the docked river cruise boat American Heritage on Friday, and alleges negligence by its owner and managers. A judge issued a warrant giving federal officials control of the ship for now. The lawsuit, filed Friday in federal court in the Eastern District of Louisiana, names the tanker, its owner Nave Shipping SA and manager Thome Ship Management, and asks that the vessel be seized and sold to cover the damage, the BBC reported. CBC, citing the Associated Press, said the tanker is owned by a subsidiary of a Chinese company. Everyone aboard survived; 32 people were taken to hospital with non-critical injuries and eight were still in hospital on Saturday. A Coast Guard captain said there appeared to have been “some type of a loss of steering.” The National Transportation Safety Board has recovered the tanker’s voyage data recorder and expects a preliminary report within 30 days. The cruise boat remains on its side against the terminal, and moving it could take weeks.
stories.why: Holding the tanker in port keeps a foreign-owned ship within reach of U.S. courts while investigators work out why it lost control on one of the country’s busiest rivers.

stories.summary: The South Florida city said a state law that bars taxpayer money from diversity initiatives, taking effect Jan. 1, rules out city-sponsored celebrations of culture or heritage. The city attorney advised that government-sponsored celebrations of culture, ethnicity or heritage that aren’t national holidays could run afoul of the law, and Mayor Tom Carney said he made the difficult decision to cancel one of the city’s biggest events, NPR reported. stories.summary: Montreal, the CFL’s best regular-season team, faces Edmonton at McMahon Stadium on Sunday. The Alouettes went 14-4 and beat Winnipeg 33-23 in the East final; the Elks went 13-5 and beat B.C. 28-16 in the West final, The Canadian Press reported. Montreal lost last year’s Grey Cup to Saskatchewan; Edmonton is in its first Grey Cup since 2015, when the team was known as the Eskimos. stories.headline: FAA lifts a rare nationwide ground stop after more than four hours, but flight delays and cancellations roll into the weekend
stories.deck: The Federal Aviation Administration halted departures across the U.S. on Friday afternoon after what officials called a telecommunications failure, then reopened the airspace at 8:15 p.m. ET. Airlines were still working through thousands of delays and cancellations on Saturday.
stories.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration halted departures across the U.S. on Friday afternoon after what officials called a telecommunications failure, then reopened the airspace at 8:15 p.m. ET. Airlines were still working through thousands of delays and cancellations on Saturday. The FAA announced the stop at 3:54 p.m. ET “due to extraordinary circumstances,” and the BBC called it the longest nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks; FlightAware counted more than 8,500 delayed and nearly 8,000 cancelled flights on Friday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed an “incredibly old air traffic control system,” saying routers “got overloaded with data” and gave inconsistent readings, and warned the knock-on effects would last days. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a cyberattack — though, NPR noted, he could not rule one out entirely — and that the outage was not related to Thursday’s Microsoft outage. CBS News, citing multiple sources, said an update to the private network connecting the air traffic control system caused it to reboot. As of early Saturday FlightAware showed more than 6,200 delays and 3,400 cancellations, CNBC said; the SEC moved some college football games to Sunday, and NBA and NHL teams scrambled to travel. Air Canada also cancelled U.S.–Canada flights, and Hong Kong’s Airport Authority said four flights between the city and the U.S. were cancelled and 13 delayed, with delays expected until Sunday.
stories.why: Air travel across the country depends on decades-old equipment that can stop everything in an afternoon; the fight over who pays to modernize it will now be sharper — and anyone flying this weekend should check with their airline before heading out.
stories.label: Reported + official statement + unnamed sources
stories.note: The cause is the administration’s preliminary account; investigators were still working out exactly what failed. The report about a network update rests on unnamed sources cited by CBS News. Flight counts are FlightAware tallies at different times; outlets described the stop as lasting “more than four hours” (BBC) or “about five hours” (CBS).

stories.headline: U.S. has lost its measles-elimination status after 26 years, reports say, as two more deaths are reported
stories.deck: A Pan American Health Organization expert panel has concluded that measles has spread continuously in the United States for more than 12 months, ending the elimination status the country won in 2000, according to reports first published by The Wall Street Journal.
stories.summary: A Pan American Health Organization expert panel has concluded that measles has spread continuously in the United States for more than 12 months, ending the elimination status the country won in 2000, according to reports first published by The Wall Street Journal. Axios said the panel made the widely expected decision after a three-day meeting in Washington, and that the status hinges on whether the same strain keeps circulating for a year or more without a break. The CDC’s latest tally shows 5,412 confirmed cases so far in 2026, compared with 2,289 in all of 2025 — the most since 1991, Axios said. Al Jazeera reported that Pennsylvania and Wisconsin each announced another measles-associated death on Friday, including an infant in Wisconsin, bringing state-reported deaths this year to 10; the CDC’s own count is lower amid a dispute over how deaths are classified. Canada and the U.K. lost their elimination status in the past year. To regain it, the U.S. would need to go 12 months without continuous spread.
stories.why: The label is largely symbolic, but it confirms measles is again spreading on its own in pockets of low vaccination — including in New York — and keeping MMR shots up to date matters most for protecting babies too young to be vaccinated.
stories.label: Reported + unnamed sources

stories.headline: Tanker slams into a docked river cruise boat in New Orleans; everyone aboard survives and 32 are taken to hospital
stories.deck: A tanker that apparently lost its steering struck the paddlewheel cruise boat American Heritage at a New Orleans dock on Friday, flipping it into the Mississippi River. Officials said everyone was accounted for and no one was critically hurt.
stories.summary: A tanker that apparently lost its steering struck the paddlewheel cruise boat American Heritage at a New Orleans dock on Friday, flipping it into the Mississippi River. Officials said everyone was accounted for and no one was critically hurt. The much larger tanker Atlantic Asphalt hit the boat at about 12:30 p.m. local time, roughly two hours after it had docked for passengers to disembark at the end of an eight-day river cruise, CBS News and CBC News reported. Mayor Helena Moreno called it “a miracle on the Mississippi”: 32 people were taken to hospitals, none with critical injuries, and two harbor police officers were also hospitalized in good condition. Tugboat crews, port workers and police pulled dozens of people from the water as the boat listed and toppled. The U.S. Coast Guard said investigators were working to determine why the tanker lost control and that it was working to reopen the river, which it had closed after the collision.
stories.why: Nobody died, thanks largely to people nearby who rushed to help, but a ship losing control on one of America’s busiest rivers will raise hard questions about steering failures and safety near docked passenger boats.
stories.label: Reported + official statement
stories.note: The cause had not been determined; “loss of steering” was the Coast Guard’s early assessment. Counts differ by source: the mayor said 180 people were aboard; Port NOLA, via CBS, said about 129 passengers plus crew.

stories.headline: Microsoft’s global outage runs into a second day, with Outlook still unreliable for many users
stories.deck: A Microsoft outage that began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday was still disrupting Outlook and other Microsoft 365 services early Friday. Microsoft said it saw no sign of malicious activity and reported gradual, uneven recovery.
stories.summary: A Microsoft outage that began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday was still disrupting Outlook and other Microsoft 365 services early Friday. Microsoft said it saw no sign of malicious activity and reported gradual, uneven recovery. CNBC said Outlook, Teams and Microsoft 365 services such as SharePoint and Copilot were hit, along with outside services that connect to Outlook Calendar. In an update at about 5 a.m. ET Friday, Microsoft said users might still be unable to connect to several Microsoft 365 products, including Outlook on the web and desktop, and gave no timeline for full service; most access to Teams had returned. The company initially linked the problem to elevated load after a number of servers became unexpectedly unavailable, and said the failed automated health checks may originate from a specific component that processes server health. It said it was bringing affected systems back in stages and extending the retry window for delayed emails to up to 48 hours. The Guardian’s live coverage said Microsoft later reported “positive results for server stability” after a software patch but still listed service degradation, and that government agencies in Australia, Japan and the United States were among those affected. The Canadian Press said thousands in Canada were affected. Microsoft shares were 2.6% lower in premarket trading, CNBC said.
stories.why: Outlook and Teams sit under the email, calendars and classes of millions of schools, offices and governments, so a two-day outage shows how much daily life now depends on a single company’s cloud — and how slowly that kind of failure can be fixed.
stories.label: Reported + company statement
stories.note: Microsoft’s explanation of the cause is its own preliminary account. Recovery was still in progress when this edition was compiled; service may differ by region and account.
